...it delivered on every last drop, with respect to its immense reputation as one of the greatest films of all time. it's the highest rated film on this site even with just north of three million votes, and (at least until now), the word of mouth was not enough to get me to buckle down and watch.

i am so thankful i finally sat down to do it.

this film is life changing. if you are struggling internally and need something to buoy you towards the future, this film will do it. to call andy's escape at the picture's conclusion a "feel-good" ending sells it so, so short. this iconic and moving final sequence will leave you either speechless or with an insatiable desire to put aside whatever's left of your popcorn and beverage, step outside, and run a marathon.

there's plenty of media out there that can humanize decadent and potentially problematic characters, but not quite the way "shawshank" can. andy's innocence is a prerequisite for keeping the audience on his side, but what about red, the film's warm-voiced narrator, or brooks, the gentle prison librarian? these guys are locked up for life on charges of murder and other unspeakable crimes, but the prison's inherently isolating nature not only offers them a berth wide enough internally to atone for their crimes, but bares out the results on camera. consequentially, you will be devastated when brooks takes his own life, and boundlessly relieved when red is finally approved for parole.

repeat viewings will make this masterpiece a comfort. you'll know what iconic scene is next; whether it's tarring the roof, andy standing up to the sisters, or of course, the emphatic embrace on the beach. yet you'll still be on the edge of your seat, ready to soak in the grandeur like it's your first viewing all over again.

i could go on for days about how important and beautiful this film is. it earns its legendary status ten fold. it is *truly* one of the greatest cinematic achievements in recorded history. may future generations preserve it and enjoy it and be moved by it as we have.

the shawshank redemption will be the highest praised film by the general public for decades to come. it is very tough to dislike this film; perhaps there are some that find it overrated, but its message speaks to anybody who has a heart and soul.

andy dufresne (tim robbins) befriends red (morgan freeman) shortly after he is convicted to serve two life sentences for the murder of his wife and her lover. he is somewhat of a mystery to red since he does not seem like a murderer at all and goes out of his way to improve shawshank prison by attempting to establish a better library in the prison by himself. he is better educated than most and his friends learn from him and follow him as if he was the lord. most importantly, he sticks to the idea of hope even after having a couple horrible years at the beginning of his sentence.

dufresne is a great character and role model for his friends, but the story's focus is on red's reaction to andy's actions and influence on the group. he becomes so close to andy that he confesses his guilt to andy in privacy as if andy was a priest. this is a surprise to andy since the inmates have a joke that "everybody in shawshank is innocent."

these two stars are incredible in the film, though freeman expresses a little more emotion than robbins does. robbins is essentially there to be a guide for his character's friends while freeman is a voice of reason through learning from his experience in prison. he plays a character who is a little bit older than the rest (besides a character named brooks) and who understands and fears the notion of becoming institutionalized.

this story of friendship and hope is inspirational in countless ways. at several times it seems to implicate that characters will give up but at the last second they make a hard turn and decide to move on and persevere. this is a drama, so not everything which unfolds is happy, but the dreariness within the film makes the case for the power of hope that much stronger.

there are so many memorable things about the shawshank redemption. it has phenomenal leading performances, brilliant music by thomas newman, its use of mozart in relation to the setting of a prison is powerful, the interaction of the characters make for some memorable comedic bits to help us make it through the drama, and the list goes on and on. and even without these factors, the movie is superb at getting such an inspiring message across, and the ending maybe have you weeping with joy.

even though this is not the greatest movie ever made, this is the one film everybody must watch in their lifetime. powerful stuff.

"the shawshank redemption" is a timeless masterpiece that transcends the boundaries of genre and leaves a profound impact on its audience. adapted from stephen king's novella, this film is a testament to the power of hope, resilience, and the human spirit.

set within the confines of shawshank state penitentiary, the story follows the journey of andy dufresne, brilliantly portrayed by tim robbins, as he navigates the harsh realities of prison life. framed for a crime he didn't commit, andy finds solace in his friendship with fellow inmate ellis "red" redding, played with depth and charisma by morgan freeman. their bond forms the heart of the film, serving as a beacon of hope amidst the darkness of incarceration.

director frank darabont masterfully captures the essence of king's narrative, infusing each scene with emotion and authenticity. from the oppressive walls of the prison to the fleeting moments of freedom, every aspect of the film is meticulously crafted to draw viewers into andy's world.

what truly elevates "the shawshank redemption" is its message of resilience and redemption. despite facing insurmountable odds, andy never loses hope or succumbs to despair. instead, he perseveres with quiet dignity, using his intellect and ingenuity to overcome adversity. through his unwavering resolve, andy teaches us the importance of resilience in the face of adversity and the transformative power of hope.

at its core, "the shawshank redemption" is a story about the triumph of the human spirit. it reminds us that even in our darkest moments, there is always a glimmer of light to guide us forward. it urges viewers to hold onto hope, to believe in the possibility of redemption, and to never lose sight of their inner strength.

the performances in the film are nothing short of exceptional, with robbins and freeman delivering career-defining portrayals that linger long after the credits roll. their chemistry is palpable, imbuing every interaction with authenticity and emotional depth.

in addition to its compelling narrative and stellar performances, "the shawshank redemption" boasts breathtaking cinematography and a hauntingly beautiful score that complements the story perfectly. each frame is filled with symbolism and meaning, inviting viewers to delve deeper into the themes of freedom, justice, and the pursuit of happiness.
in the lead roles, both robbins and freeman are outstanding, layering their performances with snippets of individuality: their small, daily sustenances and minor triumphs are wonderfully inspiring.

the shawshank redemption" is a movie about time, patience and loyalty -- not sexy qualities, perhaps, but they grow on you during the subterranean progress of this story, which is about how two men serving life sentences in prison become friends and find a way to fight off despair.

the story is narrated by "red" redding (morgan freeman), who has been inside the walls of shawshank prison for a very long time and is its leading entrepreneur. he can get you whatever you need: cigarettes, candy, even a little rock pick like an amateur geologist might use. one day he and his fellow inmates watch the latest busload of prisoners unload, and they make bets on who will cry during their first night in prison, and who will not. red bets on a tall, lanky guy named andy dufresne (tim robbins), who looks like a babe in the woods.

the shawshank redemption* is a cinematic masterpiece that defies the constraints of time, earning its place as one of the most beloved films in history. when i first encountered the movie's stellar ratings, i was admittedly skeptical. how could a film set primarily within the walls of a prison captivate audiences so profoundly? driven by curiosity and a critical mindset, i decided to watch it with the intention of picking it apart. however, i soon realized just how wrong i was in underestimating the power and impact of this film.

from the very beginning, *the shawshank redemption* draws you in with its compelling narrative, based on stephen king's novella *rita hayworth and shawshank redemption*. the story follows the life of andy dufresne (tim robbins), a banker who is wrongfully convicted of murder and sentenced to two consecutive life terms at shawshank state penitentiary. over the course of his imprisonment, andy forms a deep and meaningful friendship with ellis "red" redding (morgan freeman), a fellow inmate with a reputation for procuring contraband.

the beauty of *the shawshank redemption* lies not just in its plot but in the profound themes it explores-hope, resilience, and the enduring human spirit. the film's portrayal of life within the prison walls is both stark and poignant, offering a lens into the complexities of institutional life. yet, amidst the bleakness, the film consistently reminds us of the power of hope, a theme embodied by andy's unyielding spirit and his refusal to let the walls of shawshank define him.

one of the standout elements of the movie is its brilliant acting. tim robbins delivers a nuanced and deeply affecting performance as andy dufresne. his portrayal of a man who, despite the crushing weight of his circumstances, maintains his dignity and humanity, is nothing short of extraordinary. morgan freeman, in his role as red, provides the perfect counterbalance. freeman's narration throughout the film adds layers of depth to the story, his voice carrying the weight of experience, wisdom, and a hint of melancholy. the chemistry between robbins and freeman is palpable, and their friendship is the emotional core of the film. it's through their relationship that the movie explores themes of loyalty, trust, and redemption.

the supporting cast also deserves recognition. each character, no matter how minor, contributes to the rich tapestry of life at shawshank. from the hardened warden, samuel norton (bob gunton), to the tragic figure of brooks hatlen (james whitmore), the film is populated with characters who are complex, flawed, and utterly human.

the film's direction by frank darabont is masterful. darabont's ability to translate the essence of stephen king's novella onto the screen is evident in every frame. he captures the oppressive atmosphere of the prison while simultaneously imbuing the film with moments of unexpected beauty and grace. the cinematography by roger deakins is equally remarkable, with each shot meticulously composed to enhance the storytelling. the iconic scene where andy emerges from the sewer pipe into the rain, finally free after years of confinement, is a powerful visual representation of rebirth and liberation.

another aspect that elevates *the shawshank redemption* is its hauntingly beautiful score by thomas newman. the music complements the narrative perfectly, underscoring the emotional beats of the film without ever overwhelming them. it's the kind of score that lingers with you long after the credits roll, much like the film itself.

in conclusion, *the shawshank redemption* is not just a movie; it's an experience. it's a film that stays with you, one that you find yourself thinking about days, weeks, even years after you've seen it. its high ratings are not merely a reflection of its technical and artistic excellence but of its ability to touch something deep within the human soul. it's a story about friendship, about holding onto hope in the darkest of times, and about the indomitable strength of the human spirit. watching it with an open heart and mind, i came to understand why it is hailed as one of the greatest films of all time-a timeless classic that will continue to resonate with audiences for generations to come.

at the center of the story is andy dufrense, a bank executive wrongly convicted of killing his wife and her lover. our first impression of him is that he's a bookworm, a nerd, the kind of man who won't last long behind bars. but it becomes clear soon on that he is filled with a great inner strength, one that allows him not only to endure his ordeal, but to keep his sanity and his humanity.

andy soon befriends red (morgan freeman), the prison's top scrounger. having spent the last twenty years on the inside the walls, red serves as the film's wise old man, giving andy (and the viewer) the ground rules, dispensing advice, and trading in contraband. he's sympathetic and loyal to his friends, but being in prison has given him a cynical streak that grows as the movie progresses. he also narrates the story, and does a masterful job. there's neither a single line of unnecessary narration, nor any scenes where more is needed.

andy's skill with numbers eventually gets him in good with the guards, whose taxes he does. before long, he enters the services of the warden. and once the warden begins a program of using the convicts as cheap labor- and pocketing the profits- andy becomes one of the nation's best crooked accountants. as for the warden himself, he's an interesting character. he comes across a fairly benign, if somewhat self-righteous; his piety and talk of redemption contrasting with the actions of those under him. but as his schemes unfold, his villainous nature becomes apparent.

i don't know if there has ever been a more realistic, more sympathetic portrayal of prison life and what it does to a man. in every scene, this movie tells it like it really is. it doesn't shy away from the brutal beatings at the hands of sadistic guards, or the horrors of prison rape. but at the same time, it remains tasteful, never stooping to the level of crass exploitation or violence for its own sake.

shawshank also gives the viewer a sense of the boredom and monotony that makes up the bulk of a prisoner's life, without becoming boring or monotonous itself. it also shows the feelings of camaraderie and close friendships that can develop between inmates. i've heard that the only bonds between soldiers in combat can compare to those between prison buddies, and based on this film, i wouldn't doubt it. the little things are perfectly captured as well: the cigarette trade, the obsession with the female image- to the point that you'll watch the same movie a dozen times just for that one scene with that one actress, and of course the way that every man in prison insists that he's innocent and it's all a big mistake.

through the experiences of brooks, the old librarian, we also see little known dilemma of so many long-term inmates returning to society. despite all the hardships of prison life, the drudgery, the bad food, the loss of freedom, brooks has become not only accustomed to, but dependent on life within the walls. after all the years he's spent at shawshank penitentiary he's forgotten the outside world, and the outside world, in turn, has moved on, becoming something completely different from what he once knew. all of his friends, his life's work, and his purpose are there in the prison. inside, he's well liked, a learned man and intellectual among his peers. outside, he's just an ex-con who's past his prime and not so steady on his feet anymore.

a real measure of this movie's greatness is that so much depth is given, and so much sympathy generated, for someone who is really a minor player. his story is only a subplot, yet this film spends more time and effort characterizing him than many movies spend on their main characters.

another important theme is what confinement can do to a man's soul. after years behind bars, most of the inmate's spirits are downtrodden, if not broken. for them, true happiness is but a memory; hope an entirely foreign idea. "hope is dangerous. hope can get you killed." red tells andy at one point. but andy is not like the others. he clings on to hope, even when he has every reason to believe he'll spend the rest of his life in shawshank. he's determined that no matter what, he will not let his spirit be broken.

the ending is one of the best i've ever seen, and i wouldn't dream of giving this one away. i will say that nearly everything that's happened up to now has, in one way or another, led to this, and that when it's over, you'll be amazed and uplifted.

shawshank is right up there with the best of copula, spielberg, or kurosawa. it's the kind of movie that can restore your faith in cinema. no matter how many lackluster sequels or half-baked packaged deals the studios come out with, there will always be the shawshank redemption.

frank darabont's direction is impeccable, creating a hauntingly atmospheric prison setting while showcasing the enduring bond that forms between the two protagonists. the storytelling is punctuated with powerful twists, reminding us that hope can thrive even in the most desperate circumstances.

the cinematography is striking, capturing the raw essence of the penitentiary's harsh realities, contrasting it with the characters' dreams of freedom. the film's score, composed by thomas newman, enhances the emotional depth of every scene, adding another layer to this cinematic gem.

"the shawshank redemption" takes a look at life behind bars from a whole, new perspective. rather than your basic break for freedom plot, this film focuses on the cost of adapting to prison life and how some convicts, once they conform, lose the ability to survive beyond the iron bars and barbed wire. the story takes place between the years of 1947 through to 1966 and follows the struggle of one-time successful and promising banker andy dufresne. dufresne was convicted of the murder of his wife and lover when he is sent to shawshank state prison and sentenced to life behind bars. it is in shawshank where he forms a friendship with ellis boyd "red" redding, the "sears and roebuck" of shawshank and uses his "hope" to get through life behind bars. it is he ("red") who narrates the film which, rather than interfere upon the story, sustains and facilitates the film to make for an incredibly powerful and moving account of life inside prison. director, frank darabont directs a magnitude of remarkable performances. most notably from tim robbins who gives an exceptional performance as andy dufresne and morgan freeman who's performance as 'red' makes for a fascinating and intriguing film. fine supporting performances also come from bob gunton (warden samuel norton), william sadler (heywood), and clancy brown (captain byron t. hadley) but remarkably, one of the first-class performances comes from james whitmore as brooks hatlen. the scenes with him attempting to cope with life outside of shawshank make for one of the film's most moving, effective and powerful sequences. "the shawshank redepmtion" is a truly remarkable film and is utterly unique not just in the prison drama genre but in the history of film its self.

the shawshank redemption is a movie which will always stay with you. it has been good 15 years since i first saw this masterpiece and yet its taste lingers with me. it is not that i had not read stephen king's short story, 'rita hayworth and shawshank redemption' already, nor was it the first time that i was watching a movie adaptation of a classic book or a short story (which, i confess, as a cherishing reader of the original works, had often been disappointing). but despite having watched this adaptation over and over again, each time i suggest this work of art to a friend, i have just one thing to say, 'if a movie could ever intoxicate its viewers, this would be the one'.

the life of the shawshank prison is manifested in the story of andy dufresne, a banker, who was convicted for the murder of his cheating wife and was forced to accustom to the miserable life of the prison. compellingly narrated by his best prison buddy 'red', the movie, since the word go, engages the viewer in a tug of war as one tries to decide if the prison was changing andy or, if andy, through his submission, was changing the life within the prison. he was resilient, bold,yet non-rebellious, he was persistent, yet never imposing, and he was blending in yet standing out. thus, if andy was in a predicament within shawshank, he was himself a predicament for the prison and it is left upon the viewer till the very end to decide on the question of who prevails in the end.

but the movie is not engulfed by andy alone. it weaves within his life an account of multiple characters who give altering dimensions to the viewer's imagination of a prison life, as each character attempts to force an outcome for itself within the constraints of shawshank. yet the charm of andy's character makes him stand out for me. it did not take long for 'handy' andy to come to terms with this new life,and it seems to the viewer that he has accepted his fate. in his long journey, he makes warm relationships with his inmates and on rare, but stunning occasions, makes them see themselves as free men, albeit in prison uniform. and then one realizes that despite having accepted his fate,this was probably what andy always felt;he was a free man within a prison uniform. how else could he have relentlessly pursued his freedom and executed his escape with such beauty? the viewer, the prison, saw him caged in his circumstances, surrendered and accustomed, freed only in the end after his escape from shawshank. but the story was throughout different for andy was always free, even inside shawshank.

this classic has seen me through tough times and is no less than a lesson in optimism and tenacity. amidst all other things, it is a story about one's pursuit after the impossible. when the going gets tough, the tough usually find ways to force a change as it tells you to begin with the slightest of openings and keep 'chipping away'.

//////spoilers included////////// before i begin this review i would like to state my age and the date. i am 16 years old and today's date is july 16th 2016. i know thousands of reviews have been written regarding this movie but i doubt many have been wrote through the eyes and mind of a teenager. this film was originally recommended to me by my uncle when i was the age of 14, at the time i shunned the offer. 2 years later i have sat down to watch this film and i can comfortably say it was one of the best decisions i've made. the movie begins with an innocent banker andy dufrene (tom robbins) being sentenced to shawshank prison for the murder of his wife. he soon is introduced to the trusty red (morgan freeman), their friendship blossoms and this adds to the raw cinematography. i can honestly say from the eyes of naive teenager this is one of, if not the best films i have seen. it stems along side another stephen king classic, stand by me. the shawshank redemption is often critiqued along side the godfarther to determine which is the greatest. but personally i believe the godfarther should put it's success down to the director francis coppola and main actor marlon brando, without them the movie would not be the same. shawshank is genuine and delivers morals with a great perspective on life, that being friendship and loyalty is more important than greed and success. it's very rare to find a film that really hits you and makes you actually contemplate what should be a priority and that is why i believe the shawshank redemtion is greatest film ever made. frank darabont - job well done!

this film is nothing short of phenomenal and i can see why it is considered among many as the greatest film ever created. my favourite two kinds of films consist of crowd pleasers and deep dive dramas that focus on certain lifestyles. this film fills both those slots. we get to see how exactly prison affects people and everything that is involved with being a prisoner. we also get some great moments towards the end that put a smile on your face every time you watch it.

across the board incredible acting, tim robbins and morgan freeman both give probably their greatest performance, along side the rest of this perfect cast.

tim robbins character andy dufresne gives us the angle of an innocent man entering prison, but not just an innocent man an intelligent innocent and i'll get to why his intelligence is so important later. we get to see andy go through different stages of prison as we see what happens to people that are alone in prison, how they get targeted out by rapists and how they are treated with zero respect. then we get to see what happens when you have something to offer the guards and the warden, in andy's case it's is knowledge of banking. we see andy begin by helping guards set up savings accounts and help them with their taxes all of which help him get in good with guards. but eventually we get to see how certain guards or in this case the warden may be worse then the people imprisoned. warden norton played by bob gunton recruits andy to help him launder money, but once andy has a chance at getting out the warden makes sure he can't leave by killing the person that could lead andy to freedom. this again gives us a great angle into what goes on in these prisons and how guards and wardens take advantage of their authority since they know inmates can do nothing to stop them.

we don't find out until the end of the film but throughout his time in prison andy has been digging a hole to escape, which really adds another layer onto why he does the things he does. andy has been attempting to make the lives of these inmates better so when he eventually escapes he doesn't feel guilty for leaving his friends in a unsafe environment. we see him build up a large library as well as teach certain inmates so they can receive their high school diploma. then at the end andy is responsible for the arrest and 'almost arrest' of the warden and captain hadley.

another side of prison we get to see are the prisoners who have essentially spent their lives in prison. red played by morgan freeman has become somewhat of a tycoon in prison, as he is one of the people that smuggle into the prison. by the time red is released he had spent 40 years in prison and isn't accustomed to life outside, so when he is released and begins working he realizes that he is not meant to be outside of prison.

another character in this film had the same revelation. brooks hatlen played by james whitmore was released from prison earlier in the film but when he had that revelation he committed suicide. red on the other hand was lucky enough to have a friend like andy. before andy escaped we get to see him give instructions to red on where to find a rock, and under that rock is where andy had hidden something. under that rock was a letter to red explaining where andy was and that he would love to have his help with a new project of his. that is when we get to see the two reunite in a very satisfying conclusion.

back in 1994, 'the shawshank redemption' opened to lukewarm reviews and mild economic success, securing less than $30 million at the domestic box office. though nominated for a very respectable seven academy awards, it failed to win any of these, up against the likes of 'forrest gump' and 'pulp fiction.' since then, the film has steadily grown in popularity and now stands as one of the most highly-regarded films of the 1990's.

convicted for the brutal murder of his wife and her lover, a crime of which he claims to be innocent, andy dufresne (tim robbins, 'mystic river,' 2003) is ordered to serve two back-to-back life sentences at shawshank prison. life is hard. the prison guards are brutal and unforgiving, many prisoners are ruthlessly antagonistic towards andy, and the warden is greedy and corrupt. nevertheless, andy forms lifelong friendships with many of his fellow prisoners, most particularly red (morgan freeman, 'se7en,' 1995), the "man who can get things." clinging stubbornly to the knowledge of his own innocence, andy never loses his hope that justice will inevitably prevail.

the shawshank redemption" is a cinematic masterpiece that transcends time, offering a profound exploration of hope, friendship, and the human spirit's resilience. directed by frank darabont and adapted from stephen king's novella, the film takes us on an unforgettable journey through the lives of andy dufresne (tim robbins) and ellis "red" redding (morgan freeman) within the cold, oppressive walls of shawshank prison.

the story begins with andy, a quiet and intelligent banker, being convicted for the murder of his wife and her lover-a crime he insists he didn't commit. thrown into the harsh realities of prison life, andy seems out of place, but his determination to hold on to hope sets him apart. over time, he forms an unlikely bond with red, a long-serving inmate known for his ability to "get things." their friendship becomes the heart of the story, offering moments of warmth and humanity amid the grim backdrop of shawshank.

what makes the shawshank redemption so extraordinary is its ability to weave a narrative that is both poignant and uplifting. the screenplay is a masterclass in storytelling, blending subtle symbolism with powerful dialogue. andy's actions-whether it's carving chess pieces, introducing a library system, or playing mozart over the prison pa system-represent his quiet rebellion against despair. his unwavering belief that "hope is a good thing, maybe the best of things" becomes the film's central message.

morgan freeman's narration is iconic, lending the film a soul-stirring depth. his voice carries the weight of years spent in confinement, balancing moments of quiet reflection with dry wit. tim robbins, on the other hand, delivers a restrained yet compelling performance as andy, portraying a man whose intelligence and quiet strength become his tools for survival.

visually, the film captures both the claustrophobia of prison life and the expansiveness of hope. roger deakins' cinematography uses stark contrasts to reflect the emotional tone, while thomas newman's hauntingly beautiful score elevates every scene.

at its core, the shawshank redemption is about the triumph of the human spirit. it reminds us that even in the darkest places, hope can light the way to freedom-whether that freedom is physical, emotional, or spiritual. the final act, with its twist and deeply satisfying resolution, is as cathartic as it is inspiring.

released in 1994, the film initially underperformed at the box office but has since gained legendary status, often regarded as one of the greatest films of all time. its enduring appeal lies in its universal themes and ability to connect with audiences on a deeply personal level.

in short, the shawshank redemption is not just a film you watch-it's a film you experience, and it leaves you with the unshakable belief that "some birds aren't meant to be caged." a true classic, it's a testament to the power of storytelling and the enduring strength of hope.

the shawshank redemption stands as a quintessential example of cinematic brilliance, weaving a tale of hope, friendship, and resilience that transcends time. directed by frank darabont and based on a novella by stephen king, this film has rightfully earned its place as one of the greatest movies ever made.

from its opening scenes, the shawshank redemption captivates with its powerful storytelling and complex characters. tim robbins delivers a masterful performance as andy dufresne, a banker wrongfully imprisoned for the murder of his wife and her lover. robbins' portrayal of dufresne's quiet dignity and unyielding hope anchors the film, making his journey from despair to redemption deeply compelling.

morgan freeman's portrayal of ellis "red" redding is nothing short of extraordinary. freeman's nuanced and heartfelt performance provides the perfect counterbalance to robbins' andy, and his narration adds a layer of profound wisdom and introspection. the chemistry between robbins and freeman is palpable, elevating their characters' friendship to one of the most memorable relationships in film history.

the film's direction, by frank darabont, is meticulous and immersive. the storytelling is rich with emotional depth, and darabont's attention to detail in every frame ensures that the film resonates long after the credits roll. the cinematography, with its evocative use of light and shadow, further enhances the mood and atmosphere, capturing both the bleakness of shawshank prison and the glimmers of hope within.

thomas newman's score complements the film's themes perfectly, with a hauntingly beautiful soundtrack that underscores the emotional weight of the story. the music subtly weaves through the narrative, enhancing the impact of each pivotal moment and contributing to the film's timeless quality.

frank darabont's the shawshank redemption is a film about hope and persistence and the rewards for being hopeful and persistent. throughout this film the main character andy dufresne (tim robbins) shows that by being persistent and hopeful you can achieve whatever you want. red (morgan freeman) is a character who plays the devil's advocate throughout the film; while he supports andy and everything he does, he also manages to make it seem like his actions are pointless and a waste of time, however andy did what he wanted and did not care what others thought, thus reinforcing the theme of persistence. the film uses brooks (james whitmore) actions to exemplify the decisions that are made when someone loses hope and does not have the persistence to move forward. the sound effects of this film are key to the added sense of realism and dimensionality of the film. such as the background noises like small water droplets to the right up front noises like the slamming and locking of the prison cell doors. other things such as background music are used to set the theme of the movie and the scene currently being viewed, while the background and foreground noises add depth and dimension to the film immersing the viewer and giving the sense of physically being there. sounds like those of the prison cells, water droplets and the absolute silence of solitary confinement exemplify the theme because to survive all of that you have to have the determination, persistence and hope in order to move forward and survive. the director, frank darabont, used the cutting and duration of scenes in order to reinforce the theme and convey the emotions of the film. such as when there is a dramatic/sad scene the panning is very slow and the scene last for an extended period of time with soft music playing in the background, thus providing the feeling of hopelessness, loss and sadness. on the other hand he also uses this technique to convey happy scenes in the film, such as when andy's schemes went to plan, the scenes were very bright, usually with upbeat background music and were brightly lit. all in all this movie was done very well and tells the story while trying to immerse the viewer into the film. the story being that by being persistent and hopeful you can improve your always improve your situation and maybe achieve redemption for the wrongs that you have done.

the shawshank redemption is a masterpiece of storytelling and cinematography. the film follows the life of andy dufresne, a banker who is wrongly convicted of murdering his wife and her lover, and sentenced to life imprisonment at shawshank state penitentiary. there, he meets red, a seasoned inmate who becomes his friend and mentor. together, they endure the harsh realities of prison life, while never losing hope of freedom.

the film is based on a novella by stephen king, but transcends the genre of a typical prison drama. it explores themes such as friendship, justice, corruption, redemption, and the human spirit. the film is full of memorable scenes and dialogues, such as the iconic "get busy living or get busy dying" quote, or the scene where andy plays mozart's music over the prison loudspeaker, giving a moment of beauty and joy to the inmates.

the performances by the cast are superb, especially by tim robbins and morgan freeman, who deliver nuanced and emotional portrayals of their characters. the film also features a brilliant score by thomas newman, and a stunning cinematography by roger deakins, who creates a contrast between the dark and oppressive prison and the bright and liberating outside world.

for a long, long time i wondered what was really going on. 9.3 out of 10 possible points on the world's largest film database imdb, even before classics like the godfather part 1 and 2 and leader of some best lists. yet it's just about a convicted banker who befriends morgan freeman and gets used to his life as a prisoner in shawshank men's prison. but there's a lot more to this film than the blue-eyed setting up of modern movie clichés.

for the crux of the shawshank redemption already lies in its ensemble. tim robbins and morgan freeman as the leading men in their absolute prime as actors. secondary characters that integrate ideally into the scenarios of the protagonists and all have essential functions as their companions. villains that seem generic from today's point of view, but for those times were unparalleled in cruelty. all of these ingeniously written roles have a hand in the plot, none of them feeling superfluous at any point. of course, the film's trump card is the chemistry between robbin's character andy and freeman's red. after an initial distance, the two grow closer and closer as the film progresses, and within the nearly 30 years over which the plot takes place, they become almost inseparable. a down-to-earth and simple male friendship, where both of them share a terrible fate. how the two manage to carry each other through the cold harshness of prison life is gripping to follow. the individual scenes mainly belong to robbin's andy. this one is characterized by red's over-voice and while this movie tool works in very few cases, it's a bull's eye here. it's not for nothing that freeman's voice is considered iconic to this day. you have from the start that a man is telling his friend's story. freeman's screen time suffers a bit as a result, but it doesn't take anything away from what is arguably the best performance of his career. robbins delivers the much quieter and subtler performance, while freeman excels in empathetic and even comedic monologues and dialogue at times. the rest of the cast adds to an all-around perfect ensemble performance. foremost among them is bob gunton as the corrupt warden norton, under whose hypocritical posturing as a sensible christian lurks a malicious layer that lends the film some (necessary) devastation.

whether the shawshank redemption is really the best film of all time is debatable. however, one thing can't be denied: from an objective point of view, it is without major weaknesses. if anything, the slightly pathetic and conventional ending actually fits seamlessly with the previous plot. in this respect, this is perhaps a point of criticism, but merely one without much significance. otherwise, it's a film that still did a lot to me at 22 years old, even 27 years later. the sensations of pain, shock and happiness regularly catch up with you. despite its epic running length and slow build, the film is always entertaining and engaging, and it's also beautifully directed and photographed. hard to find any flaws here.

"the shawshank redemption" is a cinematic triumph that transcends the boundaries of genre and era. adapted from stephen king's novella, this film weaves a spellbinding narrative of hope, resilience, and the enduring power of the human spirit.

set within the confines of shawshank state penitentiary, the film follows the journey of andy dufresne, a banker wrongfully convicted of murder, and his unlikely friendship with fellow inmate red. as the story unfolds, we are drawn into a world of injustice and oppression, where hope flickers like a distant beacon in the darkest of nights.

what sets "the shawshank redemption" apart is its unwavering commitment to authenticity and emotional depth. every frame is imbued with a sense of raw honesty, capturing the pain and longing of its characters with unflinching precision.

at the heart of the film lies the transformative power of friendship and the indomitable human spirit. andy and red's bond transcends the confines of their prison walls, offering solace and redemption in the most unlikely of places.

director frank darabont's masterful storytelling is complemented by stellar performances from tim robbins and morgan freeman, who breathe life into their respective roles with a rare blend of nuance and gravitas. their on-screen chemistry is nothing short of mesmerizing, elevating "the shawshank redemption" to a level of cinematic greatness rarely achieved.

as the story reaches its poignant conclusion, we are reminded that hope is a force more powerful than any prison bars or shackles of injustice. "the shawshank redemption" is a timeless masterpiece that continues to inspire and uplift audiences around the world, proving that even in the darkest of times, there is always light at the end of the tunnel.

i've seen this movie about a half-dozen times now, and it's slowly occurred to me that this is one of my two or three very favorite films. each time i've seen it, i can appreciate different things about it, and the depth of the dialogue, and the meaning behind the events and characters takes on different symbolism and significance.

having just read the story this was based on, i find it a rare example of where the film is better than the book. not that the book isn't good, but there are some significant changes in the film that helped to make it such an endearing piece of work, and a more powerful experience than the original short story was. the development of the characters of the warden, and brooks, for example, really fleshes out the story well.

the acting and direction is perfectly subtle and restrained, and though the feel may be a bit slow at times for some people, it gives a good sense of the feeling of time slowly dripping by in these people's lives.

what a shame that this was nominated for so many academy awards, including best picture, actor (morgan freeman), and adapted screenplay, cinematography, music, etc., but didn't win anything. granted, "forrest gump" is a great film, too, but it would have been nice if "shawshank" had at least won something. oh, well, that's not really important in the big picture, i suppose. the fact that this film is ranked #2 of all time here is very telling, and i'm sure it will be appreciated for a very long time to come... i know that every time it comes on tnt, i have to watch it again!

i'm not here to tell you that this is the best movie ever made, i can't do that. movies are about the meaning they have to your life and one's personal experience defines what you relate to, thus that title will always be different for each individual, but what i can do is tell you about the effect it had on me.

first and foremost this is a story about hope. it's not a story about crime & prison, if you adhere to this interpretation then you're not looking deep enough into the themes of the film. yes, mr. king uses the story of andy to communicate his messages, but the narration itself is entirely superficial, this could have just as easily been a story about war, but the conduit he uses is fairly well suited to his goal.

the acting is superb, i couldn't think of a better suited cast. tim robbins is fantastic as andy (the main character), and morgan freeman is just as good as his friend. the last time i saw acting this good was in the godfather. you feel for the characters, not only because of the superb acting but also because the character development is so subtle and concise that by the end of the film you feel as if you've known them all your life.

i'll elaborate on the allegory portrayed. the film explores such areas as corruption, religion, hope, love & integrity. king suggests that hope is the most important thing in life, and those who have lost it ultimately decay into a sea of mediocrity (as shown through contrast between brooks & red). this was the theme i found most interesting and applicable to my life, but the rest are equally as touching. notice the difference in behavior between those who are religious and those who are not, king hints at a perceived justification for evil in the contrast between andy & the warden.

integrity is also portrayed as something delicate and somewhat essential to happiness, like hope. king shows this mainly through the actions of andy, as embodied in the quote "the funny thing is - on the outside, i was an honest man, straight as an arrow. i had to come to prison to be a crook." (that was not a spoiler, it's fairly obvious that he goes to prison, just by looking at the synopsis)

i don't wish to get into the story too much, just keep these themes in mind when you watch the movie and you'll find it infinitely more rewarding.

in conclusion, the shawshank redemption is the best film of the past 20 years, and while it perhaps doesn't deserve that top spot (i'm still deciding, but i doubt i can convince myself to concede it does), it is still an essential movie in my collection and i wouldn't give it up for anything. it's right up there with the godfather and the good, the bad & the ugly.

the film begins with andy dufresne being sentenced for life because of killing his wife and her lover, a crime he had the motives for but never did. thus begins shawshank redemption, a film i've seen multiple times and the first time was in high school. it was one of those films that stuck with me for a long time and when i watched it as i grew older, the film hit me much more with his emotional impact and the deep emotional depth it has. you see, shawshank redemption is a film you can rewatch multiple times and find something new to like, details you've never seen before, and plainly be entertained for 142 minutes. now, it has been around 6 years since i last saw the film and i'm as impressed now since then. it's the first time watching it on 4k blu-ray and i'm even more impressed, mainly because of the musical score, i've never appreciated the soundtrack before but with the dolby atmos track it just hits differently. same with the sound design, it's terrific and you truly hear the prison fence rattling and the loud crowd when andy dufresne enters the prison. the picture quality is truly mesmerizing, photographed brilliantly by roger deakins who's among the best cinematographers in hollywood. back to the 4k transfer, with the hdr and dolby vision, the color grading is just phenomenal. from a reviewer at high-def digest, "though the palette remains drab for most of the movie, splashes of color make huge impressions. bold, brassy reds, verdant greens, and cool blues grab attention, and the orange glow that bathes the picture during its final half-hour exudes a wonderful cozy warmth. inky blacks anchor the image, the bright, crisp whites never bloom, and superior shadow delineation allows us to drink in the dank, foreboding atmosphere of the prison cells. fine details pop off the screen - the prison's rusted metal, chipped paint, and worn wood, the checkerboard's texture, the contours and shadings of the stone walls, the weave of the prison uniforms, and the most delicate pinstripes on suits - while razor-sharp close-ups highlight stray hairs, facial blemishes, pores, tiny knicks and cuts, and hair follicles (even on hands and fingers)."

over the course of several years, two convicts form a friendship, seeking consolation and, eventually, redemption through basic compassion.

the plot of shawshank redemption follows ellis boyd "red" redding (played superbly by morgan freeman) who does the narration for the film, narrating the story of andy dufresne (played brilliantly by tim robbins). although the film is quite long, the pacing is perfect and you'll never get bored watching this film, following dufresne as years go by in the prison. from being brutally beaten to using his education and work as a banker to his potential. it's one subplot which has stayed with me the longest, the character of brooks hatlen (a memorable character and performance from james whitmore) who's an elderly prison librarian, imprisoned at shawshank for over five decades. the subplot comes into play halfway through the film, with his parole being accepted and what does he do? he becomes so depressed and scared that he loses it and sees the only way for him to stay is to kill one of his friends, but he never does, a scene where tim robbins and morgan freeman along with james whitmore give superb performances. brooks is probably the easiest character to sympathize with, how hard it must be to leave a place which has been your 'home' for the past five decades, and not getting the opportunity to stay. when brooks lets jake, the crow, fly away. it's like he's letting himself fly off, to somewhere better, something he does later in the climax. the climax of his subplot which goes hand in hand with the overall story, is truly heartbreaking. there's something red says as brooks leaves the prison, how the life sentence is the prison taking their lives away from them, what they ultimately did to brooks. he took his own life in a heartbreaking scene which moves the rest of the story forward. the story of shawshank redemption is truly spectacular and memorable, the screenplay and story by frank darabont but i would say it's the attention to detail and every scene he crafts, the mise-en-scene. it's his vision and the camera work used in the film is beyond excellent, from the close ups and other angles like the beating inside the cinema projector room where the camera is on the ceiling and we get to see the whole room. that's one of many truly beautiful shots. you can just pause whenever and you'll see a still photo worth looking at.

shawshank redemption was a failure at the box-office during its theatrical release, yet went on to receive multiple award nominations, including seven academy award nominations. now, it's one of the most beloved films and also among the greatest films of all time. something i agree with, deeply. it's a film with such depth and perhaps one of the best adaptations of a stephen king novel, along with stand by me. with another filmmaker and cinematographer, i'm sure this film wouldn't have been as great as it was. frank darabont created a masterpiece. the performances by morgan freeman and tim robbins are absolutely perfect. thomas newman's musical score enhances each scene and contributes so much to the film. there are also compelling themes in the film, christianity being a major one, but also another one. film critic roger ebert argued that the shawshank redemption is an allegory for maintaining one's feeling of self-worth when placed in a hopeless position. andy's integrity is an important theme in the story line, especially in prison, where integrity is lacking. roger ebert wrote in his review, "shawshank slows down and looks. it uses the narrator's calm, observant voice to include us in the story of men who have formed a community behind bars. it is deeper than most films; about continuity in a lifetime, based on friendship and hope." continuing, "watching the film again, i admired it even more than the first time i saw it. affection for good films often grows with familiarity, as it does with music. some have said life is a prison, we are red, andy is our redeemer. all good art is about something deeper than it admits." like ebert, i admire it more the more i watch it. shawshank redemption is like i wrote, a masterpiece. some of the best storytelling i've ever seen and worthy to be on many critics list of best movies. it also has one of the best endings i've ever seen. this is one of my all time favorites.

n 1946 a young new england banker, andy dufresne (robbins), is convicted of murdering his wife and her lover and sentenced to life at the shawshank state prison - twice over. quiet and introspective, he gradually strikes up a friendship with the prison 'fixer', red (freeman), and over the next two decades wins the trust of the governor and guards, but in his heart, he still yearns for freedom. darabont's adaptation of a stephen king novella is a throwback to the kind of serious, literate drama hollywood used to make (birdman of alcatraz, say) though the big spiritual resolution takes some swallowing - ditto the colour-blind relationships within the prison and the violent disavowal of any homosexual implications. against this weighs the pleasure of discovering a first-time director with evident respect for the intelligence of his audience, brave enough to let character details accumulate without recourse to the fast- forward button. darabont plays the long game and wins: this is an engrossing, superbly acted yarn, while the shawshank itself is a truly formidable mausoleum.

picking a list of "the best movies ever" is always a ridiculous and futile practice. a look at imdbs top 10 shows several entirely different movies, from "star wars" to "schindler's list" and "the godfather." the only characteristic shared by all 10 is that they are "worth watching." so, since shawshank held the #1 slot for many months, it received plenty of ranting, illogical, completely undue criticism:

* that its characters were static - simply not true. they do become moral icons by the end of the movie, but they evolve into their parts.

* that there is too much preaching/narration/"babying" - there is nothing out of place in this movie. red doesn't labor his narration because he's pedantic, he does it because he's straightforward - this isn't a college professor speaking - and absolutely, astoundingly beautiful. yes, there is the panoramic shot of the azure pacific at the end - but it dovetails neatly with the story - "something that big would scare me." (not verbatim).

* that there are perhaps 15 minutes at the end of the movie in which the fate of the characters is clear and 5 after questions have been resolved - this is absolutely necessary. "the shawshank redemption" attempts to leave the viewer thinking about ideas, not plot twists. though this is only ever argued on scholastic (rather than aesthetic) grounds, even star wars' ending would have seemed abrupt without a brief, ceremonial resolution.

* that its foreshadowing or narration cuts drama - missing the point. i shutter to think of this film if told entirely from the present - it would loose its beauty. there's deliberately a lot of "time passing" sequences. the real reason this movie has its high ranking is that it grapples with "hope" - and hope, like all abstract notions, becomes concrete with introspection, and introspection takes time. this is not a "prison escape" movie.

see this movie. think about this movie. talk about this movie. the shawshank redemption thinks and feels more than other works of popular cinema, and demands that viewers do the same. i almost envy anyone who hasn't seen it yet; the first viewing is absolutely magical.

the shawkshank redemption's - review get busy living get busy dying! is merely one of the many great messages this 1994 masterpiece has to offer. originally written as a short story by stephen king 'the shawkshank redemption' has come to be one of the greatest movies of all time being nominated for 7 oscars, and winning 11 various other awards. directed by frank darabont it stars tim robbins as 'andy dufresne' and morgan freeman as 'red'. this earlier 19th century film is delivered to its audience directly through the eyes of 'red' giving us a strong one mined impersonation of the prison and the people who make up its walls.

the life that andy once had drastically changed when he is charged guilty for the murder of his wife and her lover. made to serve 2 life sentences andy soon got to grips with his new surroundings. but one day he pushes aside all moral judgement on one decision that almost as him killed but his heroism and sheer courage gains him respect from other inmates at which point he slowly becomes good friends with 'red' the man who can get you things. with 'hope' on his side andy goes on to do great things! the movie rests deeply on the persona built up around andy. to some respect the filmmakers regarded him as a religious symbol and used brief yet powerful references to reflect on this. he would take up massive challenges helping out the majority all so that i could simply create a sense of freedom or retained hope in his life. he conveys a particular demeanour that people tend to associate with 'christ' and as 'red' quite rightly says, "he strolled. like a man in a park without a care or worry".

'character development' is a complete different term altogether in this movie, taking us as far into the unknown. darabont encouraged something different, with twists and turns in the story we are continually struck with new surprises. by pushing boundaries of modern day cinema, darabont exercised in presenting us with new, interesting but most importantly feel-good and exiting characters. this would have never been possible without the powerful and striking performances from both 'tim robbins' and 'morgan freeman', as individuals they play there separate roles with a convincing harmony. but as a pair they pitch together as if you were husband and wife, the acting is flawless there chemistry works in perfect balance and there absolute ability to grasp the audience in continuous narrative is something that is rarely witnessed in a movie.

while the characters are unbelievably amazing and the script is excellent, it's the extraordinary way this movie uses cinematography to give us a hardened view into the reality of this film. thick walls, large inescapable fences, and confined spaces all remind us of this place we have been brought to. this is spanned onwards with the common use of relentless guards marching and the heavy cell bars slamming open and shut. in a way reinforcing the dull existence these men have to live with. this is all backed by outstanding crane and helicopter shots from the coen brother arguably some of the best camera work to date, the lighting brought not only outstanding quality from the work but it helped to create meaning and build layers deep into the story. finally the editing was set at a perfect pace and even with regular leaps into future the team manages to maintain a high standard from beginning to end.

it is considered as a feel-good classic. but in hindsight thoughts four walls hold a more grime, corrupt and depressing existences. but it is the exultance of writer/director frank darabont who unlike most directors forces on the real human issues head on, dealing the problems of male rape, assault, murder, and abuse in a very effective way. but by encouraging more enthuses on the strong emotional relationships created between you and the characters darabont was able to stray audiences away from this harsh reality into uplifting portrayals of andy and his great achievements.

its quite amazing to think how such a great movie would fail to make an impact on the big screen and would only pick up fame after it was realised to video in 1995. but its success was well received and people soon began to understand what they had been missing. but its only now 10 years on that we begin to see how its success continues to be harvested and filtered through into many modern day movies.

being the cynic that i am, it's my inclination to look for the weaknesses of films that ultimately detract from their overall quality. how refreshing it is that, on occasion, a film is so masterfully crafted that i can simply take in all that it has to offer. such is the case with _the shawshank redemption_.

and with _the shawshank redemption_, it isn't an issue of the excellence of the different components of the film; instead, it's an issue of the way that all of the elements of this movie-- the writing, directing, and acting-- are so vastly superior to those of most every other film.

it's difficult to imagine two things more cliched than "prison dramas" and films about "the triumph of the human spirit." though _the shawshank redemption_ certainly qualifies as both of those cinematic cliches, there's nothing about the film that seems even the least bit tired. the unique characters of red and andy dufrense bring an unexpected liveliness to a film that could have easily been both obvious and trite-- such as _the green mile_.

because of the intelligently-written screenplay, with its engaging plot twists and historically appropriate dialogue, coupled with truly remarkable performances by both tim robbins and morgan freeman that convey all of the depth and honesty of their challenging characters, _shawshank_ improves upon the repeated viewings that are necessary to take in all that it has to offer. the unparalleled depth of this movie allow the viewer to gain something new-- and something ultimately positive-- from each additional viewing.

perhaps the greatest achievement of _the shawshank redemption_ is the restraint that director frank darabont uses in unfolding this multifaceted story. when approaching a film with even a fraction of the thematic load of this one, most directors simply succumb to the too-easy temptation to tack a didactic, heavy-handed morality statement onto the last sequence. darabont attains a rare closure; he _doesn't_ moralize. he allows the viewer to make his/her own judgments about each of the characters and the fate that he ultimately meets over the course of the film.

rating: 10 out of 10. in a decade, _the shawshank redemption_ will be grouped into the cinematic canon alongside such triumphs as _citizen kane_ and _dr. strangelove_. it's not an unmerited distinction. an example of truly flawless filmmaking.

the shawshank redemption is written and directed by frank darabont. it is an adaptation of the stephen king novella rita hayworth and shawshank redemption. starring tim robbins and morgan freeman, the film portrays the story of andy dufresne (robbins), a banker who is sentenced to two life sentences at shawshank state prison for apparently murdering his wife and her lover. andy finds it tough going but finds solace in the friendship he forms with fellow inmate ellis "red" redding (freeman). while things start to pick up when the warden finds andy a prison job more befitting his talents as a banker. however, the arrival of another inmate is going to vastly change things for all of them.

there was no fanfare or bunting put out for the release of the film back in 94, with a title that didn't give much inkling to anyone about what it was about, and with columbia pictures unsure how to market it, shawshank redemption barely registered at the box office. however, come academy award time the film received several nominations, and although it won none, it stirred up interest in the film for its home entertainment release. the rest, as they say, is history. for the film finally found an audience that saw the film propelled to almost mythical proportions as an endearing modern day classic. something that has delighted its fans, whilst simultaneously baffling its detractors. one thing is for sure, though, is that which ever side of the shawshank fence you sit on, the film continues to gather new fans and simply will never go away or loose that mythical status.

it's possibly the simplicity of it all that sends some haters of the film into cinematic spasms. the implausible plot and an apparent sentimental edge that makes a nonsense of prison life, are but two chief complaints from those that dislike the film with a passion. yet when characters are this richly drawn, and so movingly performed, it strikes me as churlish to do down a human drama that's dealing in hope, friendship and faith. the sentimental aspect is indeed there, but that acts as a counterpoint to the suffering, degradation and shattering of the soul involving our protagonist. cosy prison life you say? no chance. the need for human connection is never more needed than during incarceration, surely? and given the quite terrific performances of robbins (never better) & freeman (sublimely making it easy), it's the easiest thing in the world to warm to andy and red.

those in support aren't faring too bad either. bob gunton is coiled spring smarm as warden norton, james whitmore is heart achingly great as the "birdman of shawshank," clancy brown is menacing as antagonist capt. byron hadley, william sadler amusing as heywood & mark rolston is impressively vile as bogs diamond. then there's roger deakins' lush cinematography as the camera gracefully glides in and out of the prison offering almost ethereal hope to our characters (yes, they are ours). the music pings in conjunction with the emotional flow of the movie too. thomas newman's score is mostly piano based, dovetailing neatly with andy's state of mind, while the excellently selected soundtrack ranges from the likes of hank williams to the gorgeous le nozze di figaro by mozart....

the shawshank redemption is a 1994 american drama film written and directed by frank darabont and starring tim robbins and morgan freeman.

adapted from the stephen king novella rita hayworth and shawshank redemption, the film tells the story of andy dufresne, a banker who spends 19 years in shawshank state prison for the murder of his wife and her lover despite his claims of innocence. during his time at the prison, he befriends a fellow inmate, ellis boyd "red" redding, and finds himself protected by the guards after the warden begins using him in his money laundering operation.

despite a lukewarm box office reception that barely recouped its budget, the film received multiple award nominations and favorable reviews from critics for its acting and realism. it has since enjoyed a remarkable life on cable television, vhs, dvd, and blu-ray. it was included in the american film institute's 100 years...100 movies 10th anniversary edition. here is a film whose actors portray their characters with such imagination of their own that it's hard not to like them and relate to them. you may think that tim robbins, wearing that sneaky grin and sometimes straight face throughout the film, is a lifeless individual, but in reality, it's that muck-eatin grin he dons on occassion that let's you know, yeah this guys up to something. i knew it from the moment andy dufraine presented a simple exploit to the prison guard, byron hadley, allowing him to could keep his money instead of having it taken by the irs, those bloodsuckers. in the days following, as andy watched his "co-workers" sip cold beers, he simply sat there, grinning facade, basking in the glory of his deviousness and the formation of what would become his master escape plan.

it's the simple things like that that made this film such a pleasurable viewing experience for me. the minute successes and acts of kindness and the subsequent feeling of pride and accomplishment from the two main characters gave me, in a way, my very own sense of accomplishment.

this is a rare feat. it's difficult to create a film that actually allows the viewer to feel as if they are living the life of the character, in whatever moment of said character's life said film is taking place in. by the end of the movie, i had a renewed feeling. the only other time i can recall having this reaction is when i saw the silver linings playbook (2012), another excellent and good-feeling film in which the main character undergoes a traumatic experience and we see his continued suffering, post incident. i felt as though i was with him through every moment of his struggles.

this compelling 1994 film provides a poignant exploration of human resilience, friendship, and hope.

the storyline revolves around andy dufresne, a banker wrongly convicted of murder, and his fellow inmate red. the narrative is captivating, keeping audiences glued to the screen as the story unfolds over the years within the shawshank penitentiary. darabont's adept direction is evident in the attention to detail, remarkable performances, and the creation of an atmosphere laden with both tension and optimism.

morgan freeman delivers an unforgettable performance as red, the story's narrator and andy's steadfast friend. tim robbins, portraying andy, masterfully embodies the determination and dignity of a man who refuses to bow to injustice.

roger deakins' cinematography is superb, capturing the monotony of prison life and highlighting moments of freedom and hope with extraordinary visual finesse. thomas newman's soundtrack significantly contributes to creating the film's emotional atmosphere.

"the shawshank redemption" is more than a mere prison drama; it's a celebration of the inner strength of humanity, redemption, and the possibility of finding freedom even in the most oppressive circumstances. this film continues to inspire and touch the hearts of viewers with its powerful storytelling and profound humanity.

'til then, the shawshank redemption is the best-in-show.

i don't know what to tell about this film.i just know this is the best film i watched in my entire life.t is a strange comment to make about a film set inside a prison, but "the shawshank redemption" creates a warm hold on our feelings because it makes us a member of a family. many movies offer us vicarious experiences and quick, superficial emotions. "shawshank" slows down and looks. it uses the narrator's calm, observant voice to include us in the story of men who have formed a community behind bars. it is deeper than most films; about continuity in a lifetime, based on friendship and hope.

interesting that although the hero of the film is the convicted former banker andy dufresne (tim robbins), the action is never seen from his point of view. the film's opening scene shows him being given two life sentences for the murder of his wife and her lover, and then we move, permanently, to a point of view representing the prison population and particularly the lifer ellis 'red' redding (morgan freeman). it is his voice remembering the first time he saw andy ("looked like a stiff breeze would blow him over"), and predicting, wrongly, that he wouldn't make it in prison.

from andy's arrival on the prison bus to the film's end, we see only how others see him - red, who becomes his best friend, brooks the old librarian, the corrupt warden norton, guards and prisoners. red is our surrogate. he's the one we identify with, and the redemption, when it comes, is red's. we've been shown by andy's example that you have to keep true to yourself, not lose hope, bide your time, set a quiet example and look for your chance. "i guess it comes down to a simple choice, really," he tells red. "get busy livin' or get busy dyin'."

the key to the film's structure, i think, is that it's not about its hero, but about our relationship with him - our curiosity, our pity, our admiration. if andy had been the heroic center, bravely enduring, the film would have been conventional, and less mysterious. but we wonder about this guy. did he really kill those two people? why does he keep so much to himself? why can he amble through the prison yard like a free man on a stroll, when everyone else plods or sidles?

stephen king's books have a distinctive voice - warm, sincere, inviting - that probably accounts for the appeal of his fiction just as much as his macabre imagination.

yet none of the many movies adapted from king's work have managed to capture his singular, light, immediately recognizable tone.

until now, that is: "the shawshank redemption," a first feature written and directed by frank darabont, finds the perfect cinematic equivalent to king's style. based on the nonhorror novella "rita hayworth and the shawshank redemption," this is an engagingly simple, good-hearted film, with just enough darkness around the edges to give contrast and relief to its glowingly benign view of human nature.

like much of king's work, "the shawshank redemption" is about an exceptional individual at odds with society, picked on or persecuted for the gifts that set him apart. in this case, the gift isn't supernatural, like carrie's telekinetic powers, but moral and spiritual.

andy dufresne (tim robbins) is a gangly young banker when he enters maine's fortresslike shawshank state prison in 1946, accused of killing his unfaithful wife and her lover. though his protestations of innocence don't carry much weight, his shy manner and decency does. befriended by red (morgan freeman), a veteran con who is the prison fixer, he soon draws a circle of other boyishly likable prisoners around him, including william sadler as a sweet- tempered thug and james whitmore as a cuddly old man who is the prison librarian.

if there ever has been a list of movie that you can watch for unlimited number of times.... and have the same level of enjoyment and thrill, this movie easily will top that list.

"the shawshank redemption" is a movie about time, patience and loyalty -- not sexy qualities, perhaps, but they grow on you during the subterranean progress of this story, which is about how two men serving life sentences in prison become friends and find a way to fight off despair.

the story is narrated by "red" redding (morgan freeman), who has been inside the walls of shawshank prison for a very long time and is its leading entrepreneur. he can get you whatever you need: cigarettes, candy, even a little rock pick like an amateur geologist might use. one day he and his fellow inmates watch the latest busload of prisoners unload, and they make bets on who will cry during their first night in prison, and who will not. red bets on a tall, lanky guy named andy dufresne (tim robbins), who looks like a babe in the woods.

but andy does not cry, and red loses the cigarettes he wagered. andy turns out to be a surprise to everyone in shawshank, because within him is such a powerful reservoir of determination and strength that nothing seems to break him. andy was a banker on the outside, and he's in for murder. he's apparently innocent, and there are all sorts of details involving his case, but after a while they take on a kind of unreality; all that counts inside prison is its own society -- who is strong, who is not -- and the measured passage of time.

red is also a lifer. from time to time, measuring the decades, he goes up in front of the parole board, and they measure the length of his term (20 years, 30 years) and ask him if he thinks he has been rehabilitated. oh, most surely, yes, he replies; but the fire goes out of his assurances as the years march past, and there is the sense that he has been institutionalized -- that, like another old lifer who kills himself after being paroled, he can no longer really envision life on the outside.

red's narration of the story allows him to speak for all of the prisoners, who sense a fortitude and integrity in andy that survives the years. andy will not kiss butt. he will not back down. but he is not violent, just formidably sure of himself. for the warden (bob gunton), he is both a challenge and a resource; andy knows all about bookkeeping and tax preparation, and before long he's been moved out of his prison job in the library and assigned to the warden's office, where he sits behind an adding machine and keeps tabs on the warden's ill-gotten gains. his fame spreads, and eventually he's doing the taxes and pension plans for most of the officials of the local prison system.

there are key moments in the film, as when andy uses his clout to get some cold beers for his friends who are working on a roofing job. or when he befriends the old prison librarian (james whitmore). or when he oversteps his boundaries and is thrown into solitary confinement. what quietly amazes everyone in the prison -- and us, too -- is the way he accepts the good and the bad as all part of some larger pattern than only he can fully see.

the partnership between the characters played by tim robbins and morgan freeman is crucial to the way the story unfolds. this is not a "prison drama" in any conventional sense of the word. it is not about violence, riots or melodrama. the word "redemption" is in the title for a reason. the movie is based on a story, rita hayworth and the shawshank redemption, by stephen king, which is quite unlike most of king's work. the horror here is not of the supernatural kind, but of the sort that flows from the realization than 10, 20, 30 years of a man's life have unreeled in the same unchanging daily prison routine.

the director, frank darabont, paints the prison in drab grays and shadows, so that when key events do occur, they seem to have a life of their own.

andy, as played by robbins, keeps his thoughts to himself. red, as freeman plays him, is therefore a crucial element in the story: his close observation of this man, down through the years, provides the way we monitor changes and track the measure of his influence on those around him. and all the time there is something else happening, hidden and secret, which is revealed only at the end.

though the film is set in maine, the ohio state reformatory in mansfield, ohio, served as the fictional shawshank state penitentiary. although a large portion of the prison was torn down after filming, the main administration building and two cell blocks remained; the site was revisited for filming parts of the film air force one.[12] several of the interior shots of the specialized prison facilities, such as the admittance rooms and the warden's office, were shot in the reformatory. [12] the interior of the boarding room used by brooks and red was located in the administration building, though exterior shots were made elsewhere.[12] the prison site is a tourist attraction.[12] internal scenes in the prison cell blocks were actually filmed on a soundstage built inside the nearby shuttered westinghouse factory.[12] downtown scenes were also filmed in mansfield, as well as neighboring ashland, ohio. the oak tree under which andy buries his letter to red is located at 40°39′14″n 82°23′31″w, near malabar farm state park, in lucas, ohio. the tree was heavily damaged by straight-line winds in a thunderstorm on july 29, 2011; officials were unsure if the tree would survive.[13] however, due to rally groups and inspections by forestry organizations, the tree was found to be alive and well and still stands today.[14]

just as a prison in ohio stood in for a fictional one in maine, the beach scenes shown in the final minutes of the film meant to portray zihuatanejo, mexico, were actually shot in the caribbean on the island of st. croix, one of the u.s. virgin islands. the beach at 'zihuatanejo' is sandy point national wildlife refuge, a two-mile crescent of sand just south of frederiksted on the southwestern tip of the island. the refuge is a hatching ground for leather back sea turtles, and open only at limited times (10 am to 4 pm on saturdays and sundays), and not at all during the breeding season.[15]
