frank darabont is mostly known for "the shawshank redemption" (1994) and "the green mile" (1999). both prison films and both based on a stephen king novel.

usually i am not a great fan of prison movies, especially when they involve escape attempts (as "the shawshank redemption" does). the only exception (until watching "the shawshank redemption") was "le trou" (1960, jacques becker).

but despite the escape "the shawshank redemption" does not glorify prison life. it is more of a character study than an action movie. the central characters are andy (tim robbins) and red (morgan freeman), between whom a close friendship grows.

i shall not take a closer look at this friendship in this review. that would reveal too much about the plotline. as important is in my opinion the way the film illustrates every day prison life. i have selected three examples.

the film emhasizes that every day prison life is very monotonous. to illustratie time gradually passing the pin ups on the walls evolve from rita hayworth via marilyn monroe to raquel welch.

the film emphasizes that prison life can be very hard. it is the survival of the fittest. the inhabitants of the shawshank state prison are not petty thieves after all. when andy arrives the inmates already present yell: "fresh fish, fresh fish". that the inmates may not be petty thieves but are no barbarians either is illustrated in a (beautiful) scene where andy has the opportunity to play classical music in the directors office and disseminate this music through the sound system across the prison courtyard.

with respect to the purpose of prisons there are two views. in one view prisons are an organised way in which society takes revenge on criminals. in the other view prisons also have the purpose (task) to prepare the inmates for their return in civil society. the character of brooks hatlan (james whitmore) illustrates that the shawshank state prison falls short in the last mentioned task. in prison he is the librarion, which gives meaning to his life. when released he is nobody. having forgotten everything about living outside the prison we see him scared to death while riding in a streetcar.

the 1994 film "the shawshank redemption" directed by frank darabont is considered a masterpiece of prison drama cinema, and is a much-loved film in korea. the film is based on stephen king's novel "rita hayworth and the shawshank redemption" and tells the story of andy dufresne (tim robbins), a banker sentenced to life imprisonment for a stigmatised crime, who perseveres with hope and perseverance in the harsh conditions of shawshank penitentiary.

andy fights against the corruption and violence within the prison, using his intelligence and perseverance to improve order and earn the respect of his fellow inmates. he also secretly plans an escape, and through his persistent efforts, he eventually wins his freedom in a comical way.

the film has a number of appealing elements. for starters, tim robbins' excellent performance and morgan freeman's calm narration add depth to the film, the music is emotionally evocative, and the cinematography contrasts the bleakness of the prison with the beauty of freedom.

but the film is more than just an escape thriller: it's a moving and resonant film with important messages of hope, perseverance, human dignity, and the possibility of change. it also has topical value as a critique of social injustice and the abuse of power.

the story begins with the trial of a young banker, andy dufrense, victimized by circumstantial evidence, resulting in a conviction for the murder of his wife and her lover. after a quick conviction, andy finds himself serving a life sentence at shawshank prison, with no hope of parole. he exists in this prison only in appearance, keeping his mind free from the drab walls around him. his ability to do this results in the gaining of respect from his fellow inmates, but most of all from ellis redding. ellis, commonly referred to as red, finds gainful use of his entrepreneurial spirit within the drab walls of shawshank by dealing in contraband and commodities rare to the confines of prison. andy's demeanor and undeniable sense of hope causes red to take a deeper look at himself, and the world around him. andy proves to red and the other inmates that in the conventional walls of shawshank prison convention will find no home in his lifestyle.

this film manages to redeem hollywood in the eyes of people who feared it long lost in a dark sea of clichés and predictability. darabont shows us that artists still work in the hollywood studios and production facilities. these artists show their capability to produce art; real art that inspires you to look at the deeper aspects of life and the world around you. the shawshank redemption delivers much-needed breath of fresh air for anyone who realizes the capability of film. it proves that masters of the craft still live on this earth, and still bless us with timeless masterpieces that we will never forget.

"the shawshank redemption" is one of those films that gets better with every rewatch. it's a powerful story of hope, friendship, and resilience that still feels incredibly relevant, even after all these years. the film follows andy dufresne (tim robbins), a man wrongfully convicted and sentenced to life in shawshank prison. despite the grim setting, there's a lightness in the way the story unfolds, largely thanks to morgan freeman's iconic role as red.

the movie is packed with memorable moments, like andy's escape and that stunning scene with the opera music-it's a rollercoaster of emotions. the pacing is perfect, letting you soak up every detail without dragging. plus, the friendship between andy and red is portrayed with such warmth that you can't help but root for them both.

what we get here is a heartbreaking tale that has good social commentary. we follow andy dufresne (tim robbins) as he comes to stay at shawshank prison. he claims to be innocent but was convicted of murdering his wife. it is there he befriends ellis boyd 'red' redding (morgan freeman) along with his friends. we get to see how these people navigate the prison system and the guards to get better treatment as well as to survive.

the commentary i'm referring to is corruption. we have warden norton (bob gunton) who uses andy to launder money. there is captain hadley (clancy brown) who is an enforcer with a short temper. we get to see men raping other men through bogs diamond (mark rolston) and his crew known as the sisters. there are also the dangers of institutionalization through brooks hatlen (james whitmore) and red. i don't want the idea of commentary to steer you away if you haven't seen this. we get to see all this in a subtle way that i give credit to writer/director frank darabont.

i was one of the many movie-goers who saw the shawshank redemption without being aware it was a stephen king story, and so had the pleasure of seeing the movie without prior expectations.

the shawshank redemption is, without doubt, the finest conversion from book to film of a stephen king story. perhaps because 'rita hayworth and the shawshank redemption' (which can be found in the different seasons book) is short, and thus has less for the film makers to put on the screen.

morgan freeman and tim robbins deliver faultless performances as a hardened criminal (freeman) and a man pleading innocence (robbins), and the supporting cast of criminals and guards does a brilliant job of creating a world full of repentent criminals, cruel wardens, and (without spoiling anything) 'less than friendly' cons.

what makes the shawshank redemption such a memorable movie is that it manages to create characters that the viewer loves, in a scenario and location where you'd never expect to find them. these characters, despite their faults, have you hoping for the best but fearing for the worst for the entirety of the movie. fans of king will no doubt be familiar with the way he can create such characters, but the feat is rarely carried over onto the screen.

i like a movie that can stimulate emotion in me, and the shawshank redemption did that. there are things to laugh at, scenes to flinch away from (although nothing like american history x), and most importantly for the film, things that make you want to cry in a mixture of disbelief and shock.

a brilliant movie, and worthy of the oscar nomination it got and probably should have won.

with the many other entries already here, i won't bore the reader with another synopsis. but hopefully, i will provide the details of one scene that sticks out so greatly in my memory because of the unbelievable (and fantastic) attention to detail that is not only here but is gloriously throughout this whole movie.

towards the end, red (morgan freeman) is searching for something that andy dufresne (tim robbins) left for him. red has been paroled but the possibility still exists that he will either kill himself like brooks or commit a crime just to get back into the safety of prison. his day job (bag boy at a local grocery store) is going nowhere.

months (possibly years) before, andy gave red directions on finding something very important if red ever got out of prison. red finally with nothing else left to do, follows up on that request. he travels a fairly long way (for him), across some difficult terrain and comes upon the scene described. yet, it still requires searching and faith to uncover what andy has left him.

finally, he finds it, and opens the contents, and his life is changed forever.

what is so important is the minute detail of this scene  the location is not next to some superhighway but far off the most unbeaten path one could imagine. the object is not carelessly left under one rock, but under a number. many people would have assumed they were in the wrong place after a few minutes of not finding the object and moved on.

finally, when red does find it, he looks very furtively around him sure that someone must be watching him. he sits down, now practically hidden from any possible passers-by, and opens the object, and what he finds inside leads him to even more frightenedly glance around, sure now that there must be others watching, he must be found out, he must still be in prison.

this whole scene could have been done it about two minutes, a couple of quick cuts, him opening the box and discovering the contents and then a cut to the next scene. but, it isn't that at all, it is one of the most intricate scenes i have ever witnessed for what is a small advancement of the plot. but that's the catch. this is so important to the plot, that the scene had to be given this kind of detail, so that the viewer would completely understand what andy was talking about and what red had to discover. red for all practical purposes was still in prison  and he wasn't living yet, he was still getting busy dying.

at this moment in the movie, red (and you the viewer) still doesn't know if andy made it on the outside. he escaped, but where to? yes there was that (more or less) cryptic postcard, but especially how did whatever andy left for red figure into the story? when would andy have buried it? how did he know what to put inside it? considering the search underway for andy on the day following his escape, if i were andy, as soon as i recovered the money from the banks, i would have been long gone, far, far out of the state of maine. i certainly wouldn't want the warden walking into any of the banks and finding me there, and it would have taken several days for the newspaper to decide to publish the article and especially for the state corrections officials to come down on the warden even with all the incriminating evidence. andy needed to be gone for several months until all the hoopla had died down before he could return to actually bury the object. so, the intricacy of this scene now becomes clear as it really has to match the intricacy of andy's planning for every detail this whole sequence is so important to the story, because it's now time for red to decide if he should get busy dying or get busy living, because he now finally has the choice. maybe this movie is more about red's growth then about andy's resilience. andy always had his drive, red needed to learn it. andy gave him the courage to finally face his own demons and overcome them. red now has his chance at redemption. remember, andy didn't commit any crimes, red did. andy really didn't need to be redeemed - red needed it badly, the performances by tim robbins, especially when he tells red of his request and red imagines the worst, and of morgan freeman in this little scene are spectacular. i cannot possibly imagine any other actors pulling this off.

the shawshank redemption by frank darabont is a classic film that tells the story of a man who overcomes the worst hardship and uses his wit to deceive his authorities. the audience follows a man named andy dufrense through both the most terrible, and the most heartwarming events imaginable. as the film progresses, viewers develop a connection with the main characters as suspense builds with each succeeding event (ebert). camera angles are important in every movie from romance films to action films to comedies; however in a film that is as emotionally connected as the shawshank redemption, camera angles are one of the primary reasons this movie is so renowned. this original story by stephen king obviously laid a great foundation for darabont's film; however the film uses different angles to enhance scene suspense— something that a book cannot do. frank darabont's use of specific camera angles throughout the film draws the audience closer to the characters, creating an intimate relationship that makes the shawshank redemption one of the best movies of all time.

darabont's choice of camera angle develops a connection between andy and the audience watching him, making for a much stronger overall film. the first demonstration of brilliant camera angle is the court scene, which shows up early in the film. the camera slowly zooms into his face, revealing his expression of complete shock and awe. this is critical because it gets the audience to realize the pain he is in at the moment. the next moment of noticeable camera work is when andy is locked into his cell. the camera follows him through the hallway, and then enters the cell with him. the tiny detail to have the camera join andy in the dark cell connects the audience in a way that literature cannot. at this point, the audience feels the harsh entrapment that andy feels. the next catastrophic scene in the movie is andy's rape. the camera does something here that works perfectly at making viewers feel horrible for the protagonist. it shows andy alone in the laundry room, yet uses the single light source to show only the dark side of his body. as opposed to telling us that he is terribly depressed, the camera angle uses darkness to reveal how he feels. towards the end of the movie, the camera uses one last movement that truly stands out. darabont chose to both zoom out and tilt the camera down to give the sensation of rising into the sky. viewers feel the same sense of freedom that andy feels that that moment. the view-points of these events give the movie an upper hand to written version. although the camera doesn't put these events in andy's point of view, it still manages to make observers feel exactly what he is. each of these choices in camera movement makes its own unique statement, yet they all bond spectators to andy by stimulating our intrigue, sorrow, or joy.

camera angle is frequently used to build suspense throughout the movie which draws the audience in and holds them there. the first immensely suspenseful scene is when 'the sisters' rape andy after beating him up. the camera uses a dolly shot to fade away from the men, while simultaneously moving behind a corner so the audience cannot see all of the horrible events happening to andy. the rest of the event is left up to imagination, which makes the spectators think about how andy feels. the camera movement itself is suspenseful in its nature. the next suspense-building scene is the book-shelving scene in the library that andy took over. the camera shows andy and red's conversation from shelf to shelf, making them pause between each of their statements. at this point, they were talking about andy's cunning in taking over the warden's financial situation. each time they move, the camera pans with them, forcing them to pause their conversation, which obviously leads the audience to anticipation—wondering what will be said next. another great example is red's journey out of the shawshank prison. the point of view switches over to red, however the camera's talent of building suspense remains the same. brooks left the prison before red, and took a journey through town to a halfway house, where he hangs himself, leaving a note: 'brooks was here.' once red is released, he follows brooks' exact journey from location to location, and then etches into the walls next to brooks' note 'so was red.' the camera focuses on the writing on the wall so the audience cannot see whether or not red hung himself just like brooks. after this, the director utilizes pedestal movement to slowly reveal the rest of the room, and it is discovered that red did not hang himself, relieving the audience instantly. in this instance, the camera helped the movie build suspense where the book version would not be able to. after this scene, as the movie is finishing up, the audience is taken to the orchards with red, in search of the note andy left for him. this is one last moment of suspense because of the camera angle. it tracks red along the stone wall, but never shows us what he sees, leaving the viewer's asking 'will he find the special package or not?' resolving the situation is in red's hands, and the camera helps to build suspense until he finally sees the unique rock. often, words with a story can create enough suspense to draw a group of people in; yet adding unique viewpoints will maximize the anticipation in most any movie.

though the shawshank redemption never earned any oscars, it received seven nominations for multiple awards including best picture.this movie has not received all of the popular accolades it deserves, yet that doesn't take away from its brilliance.

"the shawshank redemption" is a timeless masterpiece that transcends the boundaries of its genre. set within the confines of a prison, the film explores themes of hope, redemption, and the resilience of the human spirit. the narrative unfolds with remarkable depth and complexity, weaving together the stories of its diverse cast of characters in a gripping and emotionally resonant manner.

at its heart, "the shawshank redemption" is a tale of friendship and survival against all odds. the bond between andy dufresne and red forms the emotional core of the film, anchoring the audience amidst the harsh realities of prison life.

based on a novella by stephen king, the shawshank redemption is a harrowing tale about the triumph of the human spirit. the story follows a banker named andy duphrane who's wrongfully convicted of killing his wife and her lover, and is sent to the shawshank maximum security prison where he befriends another inmate named red. starring tim robbins, morgan freeman, john sandler, and clancy brown, the film has an impressive cast that gives good performances. additionally, screenwriter/director frank darabont does an excellent job at developing the characters and relationships; making the audience care about them and their plight. the set and costume designs too, are especially well-done; capturing the time-period and giving the prison a real, lived-in feel.

one of the most important messages of the film is that it emphasizes the difference between being physically free and mentally free. the main character of the film, andy dufresne, is a wrongfully convicted prisoner. however, his mental freedom can never be taken away. even inside prison walls, one can think, hope and dream freely.

the shawshank redemption also emphasizes the concepts of solidarity and friendship. andy's relationship with his prison friend red is built on solidarity and mutual support. they give each other hope, strength and dream together. this friendship allows them to support each other in the process of paying the price of captivity.

to partially repeat myself, "the shawshank redemption" is not the greatest film of all time. on the other hand, it isn't standard-brand hollywood product either. instead, like "casablanca", "shawshank" is hollywood product raised to extraordinary levels through the mutual effort of craftspeople operating at peak levels. the acting, direction, camera work, editing, set design, and music all contribute, but none of these carry the film alone. the script, however, is the one indispensable element that the others rest upon, and it is the script upon which i want to concentrate. not the plot, mind you--if you don't know already, it's a prison drama in which many terrible and wonderful things happen. such stories can be told in many ways, but i especially admired the ways director/scripter frank darabont chose to convey stephen king's original story.

examples include patterns set up early in the film, such as the pro forma speech "red" (morgan freeman) gives each time he faces the parole board, or apparent throwaway details that come to unexpected life as the plot thickens. the pacing is excellent, keeping viewers interested over the film's length (well over 23 hours) by punctuating the story's progress not only with the incidents of brutal violence one expects from a prison film, but also moments of unexpected grace.

finally, it's interesting to note that in the year "pulp fiction" received so much hoo-rah over the ways writer/director quentin tarantino played with the movie's internal time, darabont got little credit for doing some of the same things in "shawshank", such as depicting the same sequence of events from different viewpoints when approaching the film's climax. (not that "pulp fiction" is less than brilliant, but "shawshank"'s approach to its own internal time was equally artful, if less flashy.)

the only things i could fault this film for are being manipulative, as well as more than a little predictable in the last 15 minutes or so. however, the previous 2 hours are so compelling, and set up so much emotional momentum, that it would take a titanic (if not "titanic") sized object to drag the film down.

there's a great deal more to be said about the ways everyone involved--actors, set designers, musicians, etc.--does their part to bring "shawshank" to life, but someone else will have to say it. discover this treasure for yourself.

released in 1994, "the shawshank redemption" stands as a timeless classic that continues to captivate audiences with its powerful storytelling, exceptional performances, and profound themes. directed by frank darabont and based on stephen king's novella "rita hayworth and shawshank redemption," the film transcends its prison setting to become a poignant exploration of hope, friendship, and the resilience of the human spirit.

at the heart of the film is the character of andy dufresne, portrayed with remarkable nuance by tim robbins. convicted of a crime he maintains he did not commit, andy is sentenced to life in shawshank state penitentiary. robbins effortlessly embodies the quiet strength and intelligence of a man who refuses to let the harsh realities of prison life crush his spirit. his portrayal of andy's transformation from a bewildered newcomer to a figure of hope is nothing short of extraordinary.

opposite robbins is morgan freeman, delivering a career-defining performance as red, a fellow inmate and narrator of the story. freeman's deep, resonant voice serves as the film's guiding force, providing a comforting and reflective perspective on the unfolding events. red's journey, paralleling andy's, is a testament to the enduring power of friendship and the possibility of redemption even in the bleakest of circumstances.

one of the film's strengths lies in its meticulous attention to character development. darabont takes the time to flesh out the diverse group of inmates, each with their own stories and struggles. from the affable brooks hatlen, played by james whitmore, to the menacing captain byron hadley, portrayed by clancy brown, the ensemble cast contributes to the film's rich tapestry of human experiences within the prison walls.

the cinematography by roger deakins is nothing short of breathtaking. the cold, grey confines of shawshank are juxtaposed with moments of transcendent beauty, such as andy's escape through the sewage pipe in a torrential rainstorm. deakins' masterful use of light and shadow enhances the emotional impact of key scenes, creating a visual language that amplifies the narrative's emotional resonance.

thomas newman's haunting score is another integral component of the film's success. the evocative music serves as a powerful emotional backdrop, enhancing the storytelling without overpowering it. from the melancholic piano notes that accompany andy's letter-writing montage to the triumphant crescendo during his escape, newman's score is an essential contributor to the film's emotional depth.

the screenplay, adapted by darabont himself, skillfully captures the essence of king's source material. the dialogue is sharp and memorable, with quotable lines that have become ingrained in popular culture. the narrative unfolds at a deliberate pace, allowing the audience to fully invest in the characters and their struggles. the film's unexpected twists and turns keep viewers on the edge of their seats, ensuring that even those familiar with the novella are in for a riveting experience.

hey there, fellow cinephiles and casual movie-goers! have you ever found yourself pondering the grim realities of life behind bars for a crime you swear on your grandma's grave you didn't commit? well, put down that stale popcorn and grab a fresh bucket because we're about to plunge headfirst into the labyrinthine walls of shawshank state penitentiary. this isn't just any prison; it's a fortress of despair with sky-high walls and even higher stakes. today, we're dissecting the 1994 cinematic masterpiece known as "the shawshank redemption," directed and adapted for the screen by the one and only frank darabont. why, you ask, should you care about a movie that's almost three decades old? because it's not just another run-of-the-mill prison drama; it's a timeless narrative that delves into the complexities of friendship, the enduring power of hope, and the indomitable resilience of the human spirit. so buckle up, because this is going to be a ride you won't want to miss!

the plot - no spoilers, i promise!

imagine it's the 1930s, and you're andy dufresne, a banker played by tim robbins, who's just been handed a double life sentence for the murder of his wife and her lover. the catch? you're innocent. welcome to shawshank, a prison that makes alcatraz look like a summer camp. from the get-go, the place is a nightmare. on his very first night, andy witnesses the guards' brutality as they beat an inmate to death. it's a harsh wake-up call to the realities of prison life. but andy is a survivor. he keeps his head down, mouth shut, and ears open. one day, he overhears a guard complaining about taxes. seizing the opportunity, andy offers his financial expertise, and just like that, he becomes the unofficial financial advisor to the guards and eventually even the corrupt warden norton. but here's where the plot thickens: a new inmate arrives, someone who could potentially exonerate andy. but will warden norton let that happen? not if his greed has anything to do with it.

the characters - more layers than an onion andy dufresne: "the banker behind bars" at first glance, andy dufresne seems like a fish out of water-a quiet, almost timid individual who you'd think would never survive a day in shawshank. but as the story unfolds, we see layers of his character peel away to reveal a man of incredible resilience, intelligence, and hope. his transformation from a meek newcomer to the prison's financial guru is not just a testament to his ingenuity but also an inspiring narrative of human potential.

red: "the narrator who knows how to get things" morgan freeman's portrayal of red is nothing short of iconic. he's the narrator, the philosopher, and the moral compass of the story. his friendship with andy offers a heartwarming contrast to the bleakness of shawshank. through his eyes, we get a panoramic view of life behind bars-from the mundane to the miraculous. his narration isn't just a storytelling device; it's the soul of the movie, offering profound insights into the human condition.

warden norton: "the wolf in sheep's clothing" warden norton is the epitome of hypocrisy-a man who hides his corrupt and malevolent nature behind a veneer of christian piety. he quotes the bible, but his actions are far from christ-like. he's a master manipulator who knows how to play the system to his advantage. his character serves as a stark reminder that sometimes the real criminals are the ones running the show.

the guards: "the real criminals?" speaking of running the show, let's talk about the guards. these guys are the foot soldiers of warden norton's corrupt regime. their brutality is not just physical but psychological, serving as a constant reminder to the inmates that they're at the bottom of the food chain. but as andy rises in prominence, we see subtle shifts in their behavior, adding layers of complexity to their characters.

the director & screenplay - frank darabont's masterpiece frank darabont took stephen king's novella and transformed it into a screenplay that's a masterclass in storytelling. the pacing is impeccable, the dialogue is crisp, and the character development is so well-executed that you forget you're watching a movie; you're living it. as film critic roger ebert eloquently put it, "the film is an allegory about holding onto a sense of personal worth, despite everything." darabont crafts a narrative that transcends the confines of its prison setting to explore universal themes of humanity, making you question your own moral compass along the way.

cinematography & music - a symphony of shots the film's cinematography and music are characters in their own right. the camera work captures the stark contrast between the oppressive walls of shawshank and the liberating vastness of the outside world. the score by thomas newman is a symphony that perfectly complements the highs and lows of the narrative. peter travers of rolling stone summed it up best when he said, "it's darabont's accomplished storytelling that makes shawshank compelling." the visual and auditory elements of the film work in harmony to create an immersive experience that stays with you long after the credits roll.

themes - not just a prison break friendship: "the bromance that survived shawshank" the friendship between andy and red serves as the emotional core of the movie. it's not just a bromance; it's a deep, platonic love story that transcends the grim realities of prison life. their friendship offers a glimmer of hope and humanity in a world that often seems devoid of both.

hope: "the thing with feathers that perches in the soul" hope is a recurring motif in the film. it's what drives andy to seek a better life, even within the confines of shawshank. it's what keeps red going, despite decades of imprisonment. hope is the light at the end of a very long, very dark tunnel, and it's what makes the story universally relatable.

justice: "the long road to redemption" the film raises poignant questions about justice and redemption. is the legal system truly just? can one find redemption in a place designed to strip you of your humanity? these themes resonate on a deep, existential level, making the film much more than a simple prison drama.

the impact - why it's still relevant despite being nearly three decades old, "the shawshank redemption" has left an indelible mark on pop culture. it continues to top imdb rankings and is frequently cited in discussions about the greatest films of all time. its themes of friendship, hope, and justice make it a timeless classic that resonates with audiences of all ages.

conclusion if you've made it this far and still haven't seen "the shawshank redemption," then i have to ask: what on earth are you waiting for? an engraved invitation from warden norton himself? this isn't just a movie; it's a transformative experience that challenges your perceptions, tugs at your heartstrings, and leaves you pondering long after the credits have rolled. it's a cinematic journey that you owe it to yourself to take.

wonderful movie, based on determination, hard work and intelligence. use of time at it best in 1946, a banker named andy dufresne (tim robbins) is convicted of a double murder, even though he stubbornly proclaims his innocence. he's sentenced to a life term at the shawshank state prison in maine, where another lifer, ellis "red" redding (morgan freeman), picks him as the new recruit most likely to crack under the pressure. the ugly realities of prison life are quickly introduced to andy: a corrupt warden (bob gunton), sadistic guards led by capt. byron hadley (clancy brown), and inmates who are little better than animals, willing to use rape or beatings to insure their dominance. but andy does not crack: he has the hope of the truly innocent, which (together with his smarts) allow him to prevail behind bars. he uses his banking skills to win favor with the warden and the guards, doing the books for norton's illegal business schemes and keeping an eye on the investments of most of the prison staff. in exchange, he is able to improve the prison library and bring some dignity and respect back to many of the inmates, including red. based on a story by stephen king, the shawshank redemption was the directorial debut of screenwriter frank darabont. ~ mark deming, rovi

andy is a banker whose life is turned upside down when he is convicted of murdering both his wife and her lover. sentenced to 2 life prisons, andy does his best to survive by using his skills as a banker and accountant to move up in the prison world. he soon gains respect from his fellow inmates, especially red, and not long after both he and red become good friends. i was never sure what red was imprisoned for, and though the story is mainly about andy, red's role is just as important. kudos to morgan freeman, who gives one of his best performances ever.

at its core, the film is a tale of hope, friendship, and the enduring human spirit set against the backdrop of shawshank state penitentiary. andy dufresne, played by tim robbins, finds himself unjustly convicted of the murder of his wife and her lover. the narrative unfolds as andy adjusts to the harsh realities of prison life, maintaining his innocence amidst a system fraught with corruption and brutality.

the score by thomas newman further enhances the emotional impact of the film. the hauntingly beautiful music complements the narrative, underscoring key moments and eliciting a range of emotions from the audience. the use of classical pieces, combined with newman's original compositions, creates a soundtrack that lingers in the viewer's memory long after the credits roll.

the shawshank redemption is a very, very clever film in that it takes its call from elder cinema, meaning it can net not only acclaim but also a wider audience. it's surely no coincidence that the first sound we hear  before the titles have even begun to roll - is that of the ink spots singing "if i didn't care". the shot pans out to tim robbins in an old-fashioned automobile and then to a courtroom where his last words to his wife were "i'll see you in hell". no profanity from a bitter man in 90's cinema, though expletives do flavour the piece, with 24 uses of the f-word and 48 minor swearwords.

a few minutes into the film and part of the reason is given: the setting is 1947. however, the oldstyle trappings of the piece never leave it: violence and sexual activity are never laboured on. beatings are delivered in shadow, or, in the case of andy's first, the camera discretely pulls back and turns a corner while we just hear the sound. note we are never shown that andy is raped, we are just told that he is by morgan freeman's narration. that's another strong point of the film, and also an historical device, that of first person narration. freeman adds a constant magnetism to the film; his voice-over a necessity considering it takes place over 20 years. refreshingly, the ageing process is used subtly, if at all, rather than using unconvincing prosthetics. a little grey to morgan's hair and the power of persuasion is all that is needed to carry out the illusion of time passing.

another interesting point is that of race. someone once told me they didn't like the film because they saw the black/white male bonding between robbins and freeman as too contrived and worthy. i told them that this showed a suspect attitude on their part as ellis redding's skin colour hadn't occurred to me, nor is it ever mentioned throughout the film. it isn't an issue that redding is black, he just is.

ultimately, the redemption of the title comes from robbins' humanitarian intellectualism against the warden's fundamental religious beliefs. but the ultimate testament to erstwhile cinema is that of two things: plot and character. it's this strength of character, not to mention two superb understated leads, which mean you can watch it again and again, even when one viewing reveals the twist in the tale. all the characters are three-dimensional, breathing human beings that get not lines, but emotions and beliefs. occasionally some  not much, but some  of the dialogue can strain towards the overly sentimental. perhaps this is what produced the nauseating tagline "fear can hold you prisoner  hope can set you free". yuck! but generally this pleasantly paced, well-told tale hits the target in it's own relaxed way. far from pedestrian, the timing of the film is like that of drinking a cool beer on a hot summer's roof, or a whole yardful of inmates standing stock still to the beauty of mozart.

the story is narrated by "red" redding (morgan freeman), who has been inside the walls of shawshank prison for a very long time and is its leading entrepreneur. he can get you whatever you need: cigarettes, candy, even a little rock pick like an amateur geologist might use. one day he and his fellow inmates watch the latest of prisoners unload, and they make bets on who will cry during their first night in prison, and who will not. red bets on a tall, lanky guy named andy dufresne (tim robbins), who looks like a babe in the woods.

but andy does not cry, and red loses the cigarettes he wagered. andy turns out to be a surprise to everyone in shawshank, because within him is such a powerful reservoir of determination and strength that nothing seems to break him. andy was a banker on the outside, and he's in for murder. he's apparently innocent, and there are all sorts of details involving his case, but after a while they take on a kind of unreality; all that counts inside prison is its own society -- who is strong, who is not -- and the measured passage of time.

the shawshank redemption is something of an oddity. based on a stephen king novella rita hayworth and shawshank redemption, it has dominated imdb's top 250 list for years now and has often been regarded as one of the best films ever made. almost every adult westerner has seen the movie at some point during their lives, yet not all that many people talk about this film, at least in my experience. it's not often recommended to others like the godfathers, it's not quoted as often as the dark knight or fight club, it's not regarded as inherently cool as pulp fiction. so what makes it so great then? in my opinion the answer lies in its quality as a whole. it's not a flashy film. the pacing is slow as time itself - fitting for a prison film, admittedly - the conversations are often quiet and thoughtful, the prison setting never changes, but rather builds up in intensity and while there are emotions and deep themes displayed, they're not over the top or hammered in. rather they're subtle, real if you will.

it's not a film that you will talk about a lot, but it's a movie that will stick with you. it's not a film that will leave you puzzled for days as you try to work through it's meanings, it's not a hard movie to understand, but you'll find yourself returning to it from time to time. and there are a lot of things to return to. the quiet dignity of andy dufresne (tim robbins), the friendship between him and red (morgan freeman), the other inmates, the brutality of the warden and the guards, that brilliant moment in the rain, the ending, the callbacks, the overarching and complex plot.

first of all, this is a marvelous, uplifting film with wonderful performances from robbins and freeman, a superlative score from newman, is by far the best king adaptation (although that's not saying a whole lot) and has many terrific and emotional scenes, but get real folks. this is not the best film of all time - not even close. it's not even the best of 1994 ('pulp fiction' gets my nod), let alone the best prison flick (i'll take 'cool hand luke' thank you and, if you include pow films, 'the bridge over the river kwai' and 'the great escape' are both much better). just think folks. better than 'citizen kane,' 'casablanca,' 'gone with the wind,' 'lawrence of arabia' or 'schindler's list' (which also could be considered in the prison category by the way)!? i'm not criticizing this movie - just the lack of perspective. it's definitely in the top 10 of the decade and probably in cine history's top 5%. that should be enough.

there is a scene early in the movie when the viewer is introduced for the first time to shawshank prison. the camera takes us on an extraordinary panorama, beginning at ground level and rising up until we see the inmates crowding around like ants. it must have been shot with a sky-crane or something because there is no break in continuity. the view just goes on, up and around in a breathtaking cycle. the effect is reminiscent of the 360 degree battlefield panorama of rod stieger's napoleon in 'waterloo'. it is almost arrogant, except that it's wonderful. from this point on, i knew i was about to watch something very, very special.

the film depicts the institutional brutality that sadly continues to be the hallmark or imprisonment, and how one comes to terms with it, or not. we quickly discover what happens to those who don't. some hysterical white-collar inmate cracks-up and is beaten to death on his first night. it is a monstrous example of the ironically named 'correctional facility' at work.

morgan freeman is another actor as remarkable for his voice as his other abilities. he is perfectly chosen as narrator.

for almost 2 hours we endure the gloomy, threatening claustrophobia that makes up much of prison time, and what inmates do to gain some little respect and make life endurable. in this regard it has a lot in common with 'midnight express'. except that here we are dealing with an innocent man.

music scores are perfectly chosen. the sound effects equally well matched. the viewer is taken upon a journey so complete and plausible - assisted by strong acting and excellent script - that when the extremely unlikely escape is discovered, we are left believing that too.

the idea that a thunderstorm should fortuitously arrive at the very hour of need to mask the sounds of hammering, and that it would be possible to find sufficient air in the enclosed sewer-pipe, both stretch our credence a little.

my favourite moment features the abscondment-on-parole of red, who goes in search of a certain field with a certain tree. after so long steeped in the dank, evil reek of prison one can almost smell the scents of summer, the mown hay. all is silent except for the whir of insects and distant birdsong as soft sunlight filters down through trees. the contrast is perfect, the ambiance tangible. these are surely the things to savour most when freed from permanent brutality.

this, and the movie 'fried greeen tomatoes' seem to perfectly counterpoint each other. they are both of equal quality and address parallels of endurance and relationships from male or female perspectives. i love 'em both as much.

i'm told that each bombed at the box-office. not enough pyrotechnics and cgi effects i guess.

if you haven't seen either of them; get busy. but watch them on a decent telly with a quality independent sound-system.

the shawshank redemption: a timeless exploration of hope and friendship

released in 1994, frank darabont's adaptation of stephen king's novella "rita hayworth and shawshank redemption" has become a cornerstone of cinematic excellence, transcending its initial box office performance to achieve iconic status over the decades. the film stars tim robbins as andy dufresne, a banker wrongfully imprisoned for the murder of his wife, and morgan freeman as ellis "red" redding, a lifer who becomes andy's closest friend.

set against the bleak backdrop of shawshank state penitentiary, the film expertly navigates themes of hope, friendship, and the human spirit's resilience. from the outset, viewers are thrust into the harsh realities of prison life, marked by brutality and despair. andy's arrival at shawshank is a pivotal moment that sets the tone for the film. his calm demeanor and quiet intelligence quickly draw the attention of other inmates, particularly red, who serves as the film's narrator. freeman's portrayal of red adds depth and gravitas, capturing the weariness of a man who has long given up on hope.

one of the film's most compelling elements is its exploration of hope. andy's unyielding belief in a better future contrasts starkly with the environment around him. he finds solace in small acts of rebellion, such as playing opera music over the prison's loudspeakers and starting a library program. these moments highlight his defiance against a system designed to break spirits. the iconic scene where he plays "duettino - sull'aria" from mozart's "the marriage of figaro" resonates deeply, symbolizing the liberation of the human spirit even within the confines of a brutal institution.

darbont's direction is masterful, employing a careful balance of bleak realism and moments of profound beauty. the cinematography by roger deakins is stunning, using light and shadow to reflect the characters' emotional landscapes. the prison itself, with its imposing walls and cold concrete, serves as a character in its own right, representing both confinement and the possibility of redemption.

the relationship between andy and red is at the heart of the film. their bond evolves from cautious camaraderie to a profound friendship that sustains both men through the darkest of times. the dialogue is rich with meaning, underscoring the themes of trust and loyalty. red's narration adds layers to the story, as he reflects on their experiences with wisdom and poignancy. the moments of levity shared between them-such as their discussions about hope and the nature of freedom-contrast sharply with the grim realities they face, offering viewers a glimmer of optimism amid despair.

the film also delves into the consequences of institutionalization, a poignant theme explored through characters like brooks hatlen, who struggles to adapt to life outside prison after decades of incarceration. this aspect of the story serves as a sobering reminder of the challenges faced by those who lose their freedom, amplifying the film's emotional weight.

the climax of the film delivers a powerful message about perseverance and the triumph of the human spirit. andy's escape is not just a physical act; it symbolizes a reclamation of his identity and agency. his meticulous planning and unwavering resolve demonstrate that hope is not merely a passive wish but an active choice.

the shawshank redemption ultimately culminates in a profound statement about friendship, freedom, and the indomitable nature of hope. its final scenes are both uplifting and cathartic, leaving audiences with a sense of resolution and the belief that redemption is possible, no matter how dire the circumstances.

despite its initial lukewarm reception, the film has since garnered critical acclaim and a loyal fan base, frequently topping "greatest films" lists. its blend of exceptional storytelling, strong performances, and emotional depth cements the shawshank redemption as a timeless classic that continues to inspire and resonate with viewers around the world. in an era where narratives of despair often dominate, this film stands as a testament to the enduring power of hope and friendship in the face of adversity.

the shawshank redemption is an uplifting, deeply satisfying prison drama with sensitive direction and fine performances. the shawshank redemption is a 1994 epic american drama film written and directed by frank darabont and starring tim robbins and morgan freeman. it is ranked #1 in imdb's "top 250" list based on over a million votes (9.3 out of 10) and is considered one of the best movies of all time.

adapted from the stephen king novella rita hayworth and shawshank redemption, the film tells the story of andy dufresne, a banker who is sentenced to life in shawshank state prison for the murder of his wife and her lover despite his claims of innocence. during his time at the prison, he befriends a fellow inmate, ellis boyd "red" redding, and finds himself protected by the guards after the warden begins using him in his money laundering operation.

despite being a box office flop (that barely recouped its budget), the film received multiple award nominations and outstanding reviews from critics for its acting, story, and realism. it has since been successful on cable television, vhs, dvd, and blu-ray. it was included in the american film institute's 100 years...100 movies 10th anniversary edition.

interpretation, spoilers:

brooks represents complete complacency with life, so much so that any disturbance causes anxiety and suicidal ideation. red also, for a time, represents this complacency. this movie is not simply a prison story, its message is generalized to mankind in general and it can be assumed that this complacency also represents modern man's need for routine - to the detriment of authentic living.

it takes an unjustly imprisoned man, andy, to demonstrate to red the life-or-death importance of hope and the freedom allowed by hope. as shown, hope entails slight fear because it necessarily interferes with order in life. andy illustrates that this fear is a part of living, and renunciation from it results in an ingenuine sort of living.

red soon realizes - given the rock hammer, the poster, and the mexico plans - that andy had never given up his hope despite 19 years in prison. hope and a sense of freedom and allowed even in prison, but not to all (music scene). for red, it takes an actual physical freedom to live with a sense of hope. andy, by exuding auras of hope from the beginning - though he would be expected to despair the most given his innocence - helps red reach an epiphany of sorts; certainty and hope are mutually exclusive, and hope is always to be preferred. the brook's path is shirked, and red chooses life in all of its confusion, because true hope is omnipotent.

it is a strange comment to make about a film set inside a prison, but "the shaw shank redemption" creates a warm hold on our feelings because it makes us a member of a family. many movies offer us vicarious experiences and quick, superficial emotions. "shaw shank" slows down and looks. it uses the narrator's calm, observant voice to include us in the story of men who have formed a community behind bars. it is deeper than most films; about continuity in a lifetime, based on friendship and hope. interesting that although the hero of the film is the convicted former banker andy dufresne (tim robbins), the action is never seen from his point of view. the film's opening scene shows him being given two life sentences for the murder of his wife and her lover, and then we move, permanently, to a point of view representing the prison population and particularly the lifer ellis 'red' redding (morgan freeman). it is his voice remembering the first time he saw andy ("looked like a stiff breeze would blow him over"), and predicting, wrongly, that he wouldn't make it in prison.

"the shawshank redemption" is a timeless masterpiece that continues to captivate audiences worldwide since its release in 1994. directed by frank darabont and based on stephen king's novella, this film is a poignant tale of hope, friendship, and the indomitable human spirit.

set within the confines of shawshank state penitentiary, the story follows andy dufresne, a banker wrongly convicted of murder, and his journey over two decades of imprisonment. the film intricately weaves together themes of redemption, resilience, and the power of inner freedom.

one of the film's greatest strengths lies in its impeccable storytelling and character development. andy, portrayed brilliantly by tim robbins, embodies quiet strength and unwavering determination, while morgan freeman's portrayal of red, a fellow inmate and narrator of the story, is both compelling and deeply moving.

the cinematography of "the shawshank redemption" is breathtaking, capturing the starkness of prison life juxtaposed with moments of transcendent beauty. the score by thomas newman adds emotional depth, enhancing the film's impact on the audience.

what sets this film apart is its ability to resonate with viewers on a profound level. it reminds us of the resilience of the human spirit in the face of adversity and the transformative power of hope. "the shawshank redemption" is not just a film; it's an unforgettable journey that leaves a lasting impression on all who experience it.

"the shawshank redemption" was adapted from a stephen king novelette about a wrongly convicted murderer's 19 year odyssey through shawshank prison in maine. andy dufresne (tim robbins) is sent to prison for the murder of his wife and her lover. we don't learn until later that he really was innocent. andy is taken under the wing of veteran lifer red redding (morgan freeman) who shows him the ways of prison life.

warden norton (bob gunton) is a strict bible thumper who together with his sadistic captain of the guards captain hadley (clancy brown), maintain order within the prison. a convict named bogs (mark rolston) sets his sights on andy for homosexual purposes. andy is continuously attacked by bogs and his friends. while working on a roof top, andy overhears hadley's complaints over taxes on a small inheritance. andy tells hadley of a way in which he can avoid any taxes. as his "fee" andy asks for beer for his co-workers which puts him favor with the group. later, when bogs and his gang rough up andy, hadley beats bogs to a pulp and renders him a parapalygic.

warden norton sees possibilities in andy and re-assigns him to the prison library being run by lifer brooks hatlen (james whitmore). andy through an exhaustive letter writing campaign, manages to gain funding from the state to expand the library along with a supply of used books. andy does income taxes for the guards and tutors some prisoners as well. norton is impressed under a scheme where prisoners are loaned out to the community for work on public projects, norton develops a kick back scheme and employs andy to keep the books for him.

a young convict named tommy (gil bellows) comes to the prison and after gaining the confidence of andy and red, tells a tale of a prisoner that he had shared a cell with who admitted to killing andy's wife and lover. andy goes to warden norton to seek a new trial. norton not wanting to lose andy because of his accounting skills, refuses to help him. an argument ensues and andy is thrust into solitary.

when he is released from solitary, andy becomes distant and becomes a loner. what he is really doing is hatching an elaborate frame-up of norton and his cronies while also planning to escape. one morning g at roll call andy does not answer and......................................................................................

this film deservedly was nominated for seven academy awards. the acting is superb. robbins and woodward are tremendous as the two main characters. gunton and brown are great as the main villains. but veteran james whitmore almost steals the movie with his sympathetic portrayal of the paroled lifer who tries to adjust to society after 50 years in prison.

andy dufresne (tim robbins) is tall, lean, and a very successful vice president for a bank in portland, maine. andy's wife (renee blaine) is a beautiful and slim brunette who finally breaks her silence about her love affair with glenn quentin (scott mann) a golf pro. she informs andy that she wants a divorce in reno which he denied her. now andy finds himself facing a judge and jury as he flashes back to a dark and drunken night sitting in a wooden area at the end of a driveway in his car with a trusty bottle of rosewood liquor in one hand, a musical tone "if i didn't care" (jack lawrence) playing in the background as a reaches for his six shooter from the glove compartment. andy's blank face tells his version of his innocence; however, the neighbors plus two dead bodies tell the other side of the story. the dead body of andy's wife and the golf pro give him two life sentences in the big houseshawshank prison!

andy arrives at shawshank with the same blank facial expression that granted him the bus ride to the prison. as the welcoming committee provided a grand opening to the bus load of "fresh fish" inmates. this single file march of leg irons clanking, feet shuffling across the dusty prison yard, as fresh fish pass by the thunderous claps, and yelling voices which intimated some of the new fish. ellis boyd "red" redding (morgan freeman) placed a bet of 10 cigarettes on the new fish named andy dufresne. andy has a naive way of thinking, along with his new normal routine of strolling the prison yard in search of smooth rocks while keeping to himself. andy finally breaks his silence after a month and engages in a conversation with red.

andy's life sentence was almost cut short while eavesdropping on a conversation of the brutal captain hadley (clancy brown). since andy befriends red and his crew of intimates brooks hatlen (james whitmore), heywood (william sadler), jigger (neil giuntoli), floyd (brian libby), and skeet (larry brandenburg), he placed a request for a bottle of suds after the rigged roof job is completed by this team of inmates. andy was able to do his "real job" again by performing banking services for every prison guard in shawshank. although he longed for this new freedom andy still has to fight off his predator boggs diamond (mark rolston).

andy is on the verge of losing his freedom due to his overzealous attitude toward warden norton (bob gunton). the warden provides andy with a few options while he spends two months in solitary confinement to reset his mind and his mouth. this melodramatic crime film will have your emotions racing as you cook up a new avenue for andy to travel down.

there are standard ways to stage a prison film and standard ways to tell a story by stephen king. but "the shawshank redemption," based on a king novella and set in the correctional institution of the title, succeeds in avoiding the familiar.

without a single riot scene or horrific effect, it tells a slow, gentle story of camaraderie and growth, with an ending that abruptly finds poetic justice in what has come before. the writer and director, frank darabont, tells this tale with a surprising degree of loving care.

there are times when "the shawshank redemption" comes dangerously close to sounding one of those "triumph of the human spirit" notes. but most of it is eloquently restrained. despite an excess of voice-over narration and inspirational music, mr. darabont's film has a genuine dignity that holds the interest. it is helped greatly by fine, circumspect performances from morgan freeman as a rueful lifer named red and tim robbins as andy, the new kid on the cell block. the film spans nearly 20 years of friendship between these two.

when andy is convicted of his wife's murder, the judge pronounces him "a particularly remorseless and icy man." he sustains that chill when he first arrives at shawshank, remaining aloof from other inmates even when those inmates threaten him with physical harm. "i wish i could tell you that andy fought the good fight," says red, who knows andy has been gang-raped by fellow prisoners, in one of the film's only halfway-brutal episodes. "i wish i could tell you that, but prison is no fairy-tale world."

when the odds are against you, there's only moving forward or turning back. when andy dufresne (tim robbins) is sent to one of the toughest prisons for two consecutive life sentences for murders he did not commit, the mere thought is enough to make anyone insane. prison life is tough, but shawshank prison gets the cake for displaying just how harsh it can be. corrupt guards, brash punishments and bare minimum accommodations are only half the picture. just as soon as he's about to break, he makes a discovery that requires incredibly true determination and hope. the shawshank redemption is a screenplay adaptation of stephen king's novella; rita hayworth and shawshank redemption. writer and director frank darabont was able to capture a realistic representation of what prison life might have looked like in the first half of the 20th century. although the budget was very modest for this film, it really looks like they didn't need anymore. a cast that consists of veteran actors helps to meld the film's respect with their performances. one very noteworthy performance was from morgan freeman's character: ellis boyd (red). he was also the one who narrated most of the film and that's always a treat for the audience.

thomas newman who was responsible for the soundtrack did a great job enhancing the scenes whether it is eerie or joyous. although at times i felt that there needed to be a more powerful theme to reflect the scene which fortunately was only in a few scenes. nevertheless, the captivating themes are something to remember in this film. memorable characters, a great soundtrack and an excellent plot all make this a highly recommended movie to watch. there really isn't much to nit-pick about this film which is what really brings it to the top. like all highly rated/regarded films, there tends to be some form of overrating which is understandable, since all great things attract jealousy.

what is there to say about the shawshank redemption? clearly there is a reason for it's widespread popularity, and thankfully that praise is warranted. while far from the best film i've ever seen (it currently holds the #1 spot on imdb), i can't argue against it being a great film. in particular, the performances by tim robbins and morgan freeman are inspiring enough to power the film through it's slower passages. the cinematography has been praised for good reason as well, a lot of thought was obviously put into every shot to convey a certain feeling or message. although i found the story arc to be somewhat predictable, the art of storytelling is the real star here, guiding us through themes that are masterfully simple on the surface, but have a lot going on underneath for you to think about later on. really the only thing that held this film back for me is it's reliance on some rather cliché (at least at this point in time) plot developments amidst it's middle act. being objective though, it's hard to tell whether that is the fault of the way it was crafted, or just the result of the film being so broad in it's scope. either way, it stands the test of time as a film very much worth viewing. maybe we have been looking at shawshank all wrong. maybe it's not so amazing because of how many people think it's great, maybe it's because of how few people there are that don't. it certainly has a message that everyone can appreciate.

the short novel by stephen king has been adapted by owen o'neill and dave johns and is likely to prove popular with fans of the film as well as those who are too young to remember the original format. based on the 1982 novella rita hayworth and the shawshank redemption, the play examines desperation, injustice, friendship and hope behind the bars of a maximum security facility. the 1994 feature film, regularly voted britain's favourite ever movie, starred tim robbins and morgan freeman and was nominated for seven academy awards. two of tv's best loved leading men, ian kelsey (doctors, casualty and emmerdale) and patrick robinson (casualty, midsomer murders), star in this new production of the shawshank redemption, which is running at milton keynes theatre until saturday. despite protests of his innocence, andy dufresne is handed a double life sentence for the brutal murder of his wife and her lover. incarcerated at the notorious shawshank facility, he quickly learns that no one can survive alone. andy strikes up an unlikely friendship with the prison fixer red, and things take a slight turn for the better. however, when warden stammas decides to bully andy into subservience and exploit his talents for accountancy, a desperate plan is quietly hatched. a minimalist set is the perfect backdrop as the story unfolds in the confines of the prison walls. dim lighting with the sound of doors slamming and keys turning makes you feel as though you were inside the 'shank' with the inmates. the onstage partnership of kelsey and robinson has a genuine warmth to it, and this is complimented by their co-stars who bring both light and shade to the performance. no one can miss the distinctive laugh of rooster, wonderfully but hauntingly captured by leigh jones, and ian barritt as brooksie and george evans as tommy williams shine in their 'darkest' moments. owen o'neill is perfect for the role of warden stammas, chillingly bringing a sense of fear to the stage every time he features. with the film's cult status, some die-hard fans may not like the fast-pace of the stage adaptation, which takes you through the years inside at a much quicker pace than the original film. but there is no harm in breathing new life into a classic and if you loved the film, why not indulge yourself in re-living it in a new format. the show contains strong language and adult content and is recommended for people aged 15 and over.

the shawshank redemption is a cinematic masterpiece that has captivated audiences for decades. this poignant drama, directed by frank darabont, delves into the depths of human resilience, the power of hope, and the enduring bonds of friendship. set within the confines of shawshank state penitentiary, the film follows the story of andy dufresne (tim robbins), a banker wrongfully convicted of murder, and his unlikely friendship with red (morgan freeman), a seasoned inmate.

one of the film's greatest strengths lies in its ability to create a richly detailed world within the prison walls. darabont masterfully captures the harsh realities of prison life, from the oppressive regime of the guards to the camaraderie among inmates. the bleakness of the setting is juxtaposed with moments of quiet beauty and unexpected humor, adding depth and nuance to the narrative.

tim robbins delivers a powerful performance as andy dufresne, a man who never loses his spirit, even in the face of adversity. his portrayal of a man wrongfully imprisoned is both heartbreaking and inspiring. morgan freeman, as the wise and worldly red, provides a steady anchor to the film, his narration guiding the audience through the story with a sense of both weariness and hope.

the film's exploration of themes such as hope, redemption, and the human spirit is both profound and timeless. andy's unwavering belief in his own innocence and his determination to find a way out of shawshank serve as a beacon of hope for both himself and those around him. red's gradual transformation from a cynical inmate to a man capable of love and compassion is equally moving.

the film's pacing is deliberate, allowing the story to unfold at a measured pace. this deliberate approach allows the audience to fully immerse themselves in the world of shawshank and connect with the characters on a deeper level. the film's climax, a thrilling and suspenseful escape, is a testament to the power of human ingenuity and the enduring nature of hope.

the shawshank redemption is a film that resonates with audiences on a profound level. its exploration of universal themes, combined with its stellar performances and masterful direction, has solidified its place as one of the greatest films of all time. it is a film that will continue to inspire and move audiences for generations to come.

key themes and analysis

hope and perseverance: andy's unwavering belief in his innocence and his determination to find a way out of shawshank serve as a powerful testament to the human spirit. his ability to maintain hope in the face of adversity inspires others to never give up.

friendship and redemption: the bond between andy and red is one of the most heartwarming aspects of the film. their friendship transcends the harsh realities of prison life and provides a source of solace and support for both men.

the power of knowledge: andy's pursuit of knowledge and his ability to use it to his advantage highlights the transformative power of education. his self-education not only helps him to survive but also empowers him to take control of his own destiny.

the nature of time: the film's exploration of the passage of time and the impact it has on individuals is a poignant reminder of the fleeting nature of life. the cyclical nature of the seasons mirrors the cyclical nature of human existence, emphasizing the importance of living in the present moment.

the importance of human connection: the film underscores the importance of human connection and the power of empathy. the relationships between the inmates, as well as between the inmates and the guards, highlight the complexities of human nature and the potential for both good and evil.

the film's cinematography is stunning, capturing the bleak beauty of the prison setting and the lushness of the natural world outside. the use of color and light is particularly effective, highlighting the stark contrast between the confined world of shawshank and the freedom of the outside world.

the sound design is equally impressive, creating a sense of both isolation and community. the haunting score, composed by thomas newman, perfectly complements the film's mood and adds to its emotional impact.

hope. it is the single most powerful human emotion. it can keep you alive, and it can destroy your life. hope can be the one thing left in a world where everything else is taken from you- and the shawshank redemption is the perfect artistic visualization of the tremendous power that hope can have over someone who has lost everything else.

the opening scene introduces us to a young and successful banker named andy dufresne, and the things that have transpired to destroy his life. we can't help but feel sympathy toward a man who finds out that his wife is having an affair, and then gets convicted for the double homicide of his wife and her lover- when he is innocent of the crime. taken to shawshank prison for two life sentences, andy has had his entire life taken from him in a spiral of terrible events. it only gets worse at the prison, as the brutality of the prison guards is unbridled, and a few inmates make his life hell. however, andy continually surprises the audience with his resilience and his character finds ways to amaze the inmates, the guards, the warden, and the audience. the story itself is not wholly original or groundbreaking, and there is no 'surprise-ending' or major twists that come out of nowhere to shock the audience. however, it is in the delivery of the story that this film excels beyond all others.

every aspect of this movie compliments the incredible script written by frank darabont that was based on stephen king's novella. the music is a composition of slow-moving and peaceful ballads that bring out just how long-winded a life sentence in prison can be, and how undaunted andy is by the terrible environment he is in. the cameras move slowly and steadily, repeatedly scanning the prison and also emphasizing the endless span that life in prison truly is. on the artistic side, the movie is something to behold. but ultimately, what brings the entire movie together is the beautifully written and exceptionally delivered narration of morgan freeman, playing a fellow inmate named ellis 'red' redding. not only are we given a view into andy's character through this man's observations, but we also see how red himself changes his life as a result of andy dufresne.

the amazing thing about this film is how every detail in the entire movie somehow contributes to the story on the whole. it takes a few times of viewing before you can really appreciate just how intricate the plot is- how every single moment helps increase the power of the incredible ending sequence. it is not too complex, with many tangents that end up confusing the viewer. instead, it runs with a simple theme and adds to it with everything that is depicted. the only negative thing i have to say about this movie is that the ending seems a bit drawn out, but by this time you are so enthralled and satisfied as a viewer that it should not pose a problem.

a great story, told flawlessly, with a powerful message. there is not a lot more that you could ask for in a movie. entertaining and inspiring. deep, yet not complicated. a message delivered with undeniable power, and an excellent movie experience overall. if you have ever felt like everything has been taken from you, then learn from andy dufresne. 'there's something inside that they can't get to, that they can't touch. it's yours.' hope. it can set you free.

i hadn't watched this film in its entirety in probably 10 years so i felt it was time for a re-watch. it still holds up as one of my favourite films from the 90's. the very intricate adaptation of king's work is so smartly done by frank darabont. you have to pay attention to all the little details in order to make sense of the film at the end. its no easy task as the movie can move at a snails pace at times, but that's what makes it so great. its not trying to be flashy, its trying to portray a very realistic view inside a mid 20th century new england prison. you come to feel for every single one of these characters and most importantly understand their motivations. a film like this could have went so badly, but the actors and darabont seem to make it look effortless. the cast as an ensemble works wonderfully and morgan freeman quite possibly gives the best performance of his career.

in many ways, i am more than a little shocked at the overwhelming popularity of the shawshank redemption. i am not in anyway saying that it is a bad film, in fact its a great film. however, i never thought shawshank would appeal to so many people. it just seems odd that it has received over 112,000 votes (more than the godfather) and it is #2 on the imdb top 250 list. i do not think it deserves this high position but it is nice to see the film get alot of notice.

shawshank deserves high marks in these categories: directing, acting, cinematography, and writing. this was the debut feature for frank darabont and he chooses to let shawshank unravel at a slow pace. this is the perfect choice for the film. it moves slow but it is nevertheless compelling. there is only one time when the slow pace actually interferes with the film.

andy dufresne (tim robbins), a successful banker, is convicted for the murder of his wife and her lover. the judge describes andy as cold and sends him to the shawshank prison to serve two life sentences. andy, however, maintains his innocence, despite the fact that he was seen at the murder scene carrying a weapon.

in prison, andy eventually gains the respect of his inmates, including the influential prisoner 'red' (morgan freeman) who 'gets things' for the prisoners. later, andy's knowledge of finance gains him popularity with the cruel prison guards and the warden (bob gunton).

the development of the friendship between red and andy is one of the focal points of the film as each man learns from the other. several subplots are nicely intertwined into the film, none better than the story of old brooks hatlen (james whitmore) and his release from prison. having spent so much time at shawshank, brooks has become 'institutionalised' i.e. so attached to prison that he cannot cope in the outside world. the sense of helplessness and solitude brooks feels when released is one of the films most genuinely emotional moments.
