in a summer of comic book movies, deciding which one was the best is a hard task. so far we have been treated to film adaptations of iron man, the incredible hulk and a hellboy sequel, all of which were very good. the dark knight makes the decision even harder.

christopher nolan's sequel to the already excellent batman begins is better than the original, better than all four burton/schumaker films combined, and better than other comic book films such as every superman movie ever made. christian bale returns as the caped crusader, reprising the role that made him a star. bale once again blows us all away as he makes michael keaton look like george clooney in the batsuit. however, there is a reason the word "batman" is not in the title: this movie belongs to not batman, but the joker. the late heath ledger makes his presence felt in his final film. compared to ledger's joker, jack nicholson's portrayal of the clown prince of crime in tim burton's 1989 version of batman is the equivalent of the disaster that was arnold schwarzenegger as mr freeze in batman and robin.

the film picks up a few months after "begins". gotham city (a thinly disguised chicago) is becoming safer thanks to the efforts of batman, good cop jim gordon (gary oldman), and new gotham da harvey dent (aaron eckhart). the real batman, bruce wayne, is facing some problems in social life, much like peter parker in spider man 2. dent is currently dating bruce's childhood sweetheart rachel dawes (maggie gyllhanall who replaces katie holmes). gotham is suddenly threatened by the joker, a sadistic killer who wears clown makeup and gets a kick out of torture. when nicholson did the role, he went for laughs. ledger does the same. the only difference is when jack tried to be funny, he did silly things like point a gun with an outrageously long barrel. when heath tries to be funny he does magic. he makes a pencil disappear! wanna know how he does it, kids? he puts the pencil on the table, then throws a guy head-on into the pencil! sir michael caine and morgan freeman reprise their respective roles as alfred and lucius fox. both are a couple of the greatest actors we have ever seen, and are not afraid to demonstrate. they both are the voice of reason in bruce wayne's crazy brain, and crack out the funny one liners to lighten the mood of this dark film.

speaking of the film's darkness, it's not a great idea to bring the kiddies to this one. this is darker than all of the previous five and even some adults may be affected by ledger's death when viewing this film. it's impossible not to think of heath's passing when he is on screen, and some images seem a bit disturbing due to his death. for example, there is one scene where the joker hides in a body bag to avoid some rival gangsters.

ledger, once again, makes this film. fans, like myself, will love his memorable quotes such as "why so serious?" or "let's put a smile on that face!". however, sometimes ledger makes his presence felt by not saying a word at all. for example, a scene where the joker, dressed in as a nurse, blows up a hospital, is made funny in a sick way. heath simply walks through the crumbling building as explosions go off behind him. after a while they stop. ledger, makes a few funny faces, messes around with a controller, then casually walks away as the building explodes.

ledger couldn't have done it without a little help, though. oldman's gordon is given a much bigger role in the film, much to the viewer's delight. while everybody loved oldman is "begins", "tdk" establishes gordon as the greatest hero in gotham not named batman. eckhart is great as dent, and even better as the villainous two-face, who dent becomes when his face is horribly scarred by the joker. eckhart makes fans forget about batman forever, where tommy lee jones completely butchered the part.

sadly, though, the film is not without its few flaws. gyllanhall has no chemistry on screen with anyone, not even bale. katie holmes is, surprisingly, missed. caine is very good, but his role is made smaller in this film. and finally, one of the things that made "begins" so good was cillian murphy's scarecrow. sadly, scarecrow makes only a quick appearance that has almost nothing to do with the plot. he is, however, spared, leaving scarecrow fans, like myself, hopeful.

overall, the dark knight makes us love the comic book film even more. it also gives us a tragic reminder...we are definitely going to miss heath ledger.

i awarded this film 9/10 because i just can't endorse this film being the #1 film of all time.

however, it's one of the most satisfying theatrical experiences i've ever undergone. it's actually incredible what nolan's achieved with this film. batman begins was terrific, and i'd insist on seeing that before the dark knight as it repositions the batman character from a campy one-dimensional characateur to a complex, fascinating, credible and multi-dimensional subject. having established the core elements of this character with bb, the dark knight is a terrific bit of character exposition bound up in one of the best action movies i've ever seen.

the joker was apparently always intended to be the anti-batman. nolan really explores that in this film. harvey dent and gotham city serve as metaphors and litmus tests for the 'good/evil' dichotomy that are central. the grotesque nature of all the characters is handled so superbly, that you forget this is an adaptation of a comic and almost suggests the comics themselves should be revisited as serious pieces of literature. this film surpasses the comic book ethic and becomes more like a modern shakespearean tragedy. the genius of it is that it works as a comic book adaptation (with satisfying sincerity to the subject matter) but also works as an independent study. realistically, there are better character studies out there, but those tend to be those that focus all energy on that study, at the expense of satisfying the other other requirements of film.

this contains some of the best action, effects, set-pieces that i've seen in a film. some of the heist scenes and chase scenes beat anything i've seen elsewhere. most heist movies fall into the trap of being contrived, smug and pseudo-unpredictable (e.g. ocean's 11). this one feels like something conceived of a reckless mind. the film's sequences really feel the product of an impulsive and reckless psychopath and adeptly cultivates the feeling of impotence of the hero. brilliant. the joker genuinely feels like an invulnerable nemesis. as an action movie this is really outstanding. there is some terrific violent scenes and stunts that will delight any thrill junkie, and there was no overdependance on cgi.

the script was impeccable and i'm sure will work with all levels of viewer without being patronising. the performances were terrific. bale and ledger steal the show, though the latter really is brilliant. watching this you get a real sense of shame that you won't ever see him reprise the role. ledger is absolutely magnetic. hilarious, terrifying, menacing but also tragic. he really does blow jack nicholson out of the water and the third time you see him on screen you'll feel nostalgic about his loss. the supporting cast are exemplary (i was impressed by eckhart too, having previously written him off), and you get the same quality performance from the likes of oldman, freeman etc. as you'd expect.

the cinematography is superb. i saw this on the imax (do so if you can) and it was stunning, the relevance of the film aided by the portrayal of a real gotham. the pace and plot are terrific and keep you gripped for the duration. there is also a healthy dose of humour and social commentary that is all impressively appropriate. even the soundtrack is absolutely on point.

i can't hail this as the best film i've ever seen, but it so so good and if the next can improve on this, then that may well have a justified claim. it's a true shame that ledger as joker won't be involved.

batman is back. and so is director christoperh nolan who directed the amazing batman begins. as someone who thoroughly enjoyed nolan's previous batman film, i felt confident he'd never be able to surpass it. i was horribly wrong.

the dark sets. the amazing acting (with one exception). the wonderful dialogue. it was a sheer joy to watch. and the fact that it was 152 minutes long didn't bother me in the slightest. the action was practically nonstop with enough plot twists, explosions, and funny lines to make one cringe and laugh at the same time.

the big question, though, on many people's minds (including my own before i watched it) was "is heath ledger's performance that good or are the critics just being nice after ledger's unfortunate death?" hollywood has a history of doing this where they honor someone for an achievement that really wasn't deserved, but they felt sorry for the performer's family, etc. and decided to throw them a bone by overly-praising a performance or a life that wasn't particularly notable. i was concerned that this might be the case for ledger's joker. but my worries were immediately stripped away as soon as the joker made his appearance. creepy. funny. line delivery that'll blow your mind ("see, i'm not a monster...i'm just ahead of the curve."). ledger's performance put all others in his shadow (yes that includes christian bale, michael caine, aaron eckhart and gary oldman).

christian bale (3:10 to yuma) has now become synonymous with what batman means to movie-goers and comic book fans alike. he plays the cocky, rich, and uncompromising bruce wayne with the perfect amount of grace and toughness the role deserves. the only downside is his heavily whispered batman voice that grates on the nerves after a short while.

michael caine (children of men) and gary oldman (harry potter) reprise their roles and do so with the talent we've all come to expect from these two fine actors. morgan freeman (gone baby gone) returns as lucius fox, batman's weapons designer and conscious. although not particularly riveting, his performance did help move the plot along.

an addition to the cast was introduced with the arrival of harvey dent/two-face (aaron eckhart, conversations with other women). exquisitely incorporated into the story, the uncovering of two-face's origins is masterfully pulled into the story and given ample screen time.

the only less-than-stellar performance came from maggie gyllenhaal (stranger than ficiton) who replaced katie holmes (first daughter) in the role of rachel dawes, bruce wayne's love interest. although no fan of katie holmes, i found gyllenhaal's performance to be relatively unmoving in comparison to the rest of the cast. that's probably not a knock against gyllenhaal considering the entire production held some of the strongest roles i've seen this year. but no one came close to ledger and his wonderful performance, least of all gyllenhaal.

if you're looking for the action film of the year with one of the best performances by an actor that is no longer with us, the dark knight is the ticket. no jokin'.

i just followed this sequel to the batman begins. i must admit, i was left a bit disappointed. i'll tell why. the main reason probably is enormously high rating to the dark knight. i liked the first movie. it was very good. but my expectations were much more higher to the sequel. i still liked it much though. and i rate this high but definitely not into top 10. i even think batman begins was slightly better.

cast was extremely good. christian bale did his job and yet again i must say michael keaton remains the best batman. old foxes morgan freeman and michael caine seemed good again. but the best performance goes to heath ledger. a naturally gifted and talented young actor who's life was cut short unfortunately. all eyes were him. and he delivered. a worthy oscar winner.

if i'm honest, this film is a bit overrated but that's a logical reaction to heaths leaving. i suggest you to see that. the last memorable performance by him.

the dark knight (2008)-

as with 'batman begins' the first ten minutes hooks you in properly and with far more effect than the "other" four. and it's hard not to compare these newer incarnations with those first films, because they were just so bad and these new ones aren't at all.

it's a shame that with 'batman vs superman' (2016) and 'justice league' (2017) it looks as if they're going back to a more cartoon like style.

we will have to see what robert pattinson's portrayal offers in 2022, but i don't expect much.

and it's odd to think that i didn't bother with the christopher nolan three when they were released, because of my distaste for mr bale. however, he surprised me so much, but then i do wonder whether the films would have been just as successful with another actor, as long as the production and direction was the same. i don't wish to take anything away from him, because i really do rate these films and his version of the "knight", but my mind likes to ponder things sometimes. who else could have done the stories the same justice or more?

what's also good about this film, as well as it's predecessor, is how they were actually about batman, where the previous films didn't really achieve that and yet that focus still didn't diminish the inclusion of the joker and the story of harvey dent, who both appeared.

the series so far has been cleverly conceived, because they established the title character properly in 'batman begins' (2005), so this second film was able to show him at his best, having learned his lessons. it pitted him against the joker, who was shown effectively and appropriately, in a new, but ideal style.

the origin of harvey dent was also thoughtfully portrayed too. you can really see how he changed and why, unlike that god awful representation of him in 'batman forever' (1995). aaron eckhart probably doesn't get enough praise for his performance, so overshadowed as he was by the films main villain and the subsequent publicity of their real life demise, but he does do justice to his role as well.

the fact that the joker was played superbly by heath ledger can never be in question. he really brought something fantastic to the role and proved that some people just get their kicks causing trouble for no reason but their own amusement. he was perfect in the role as far as i'm concerned. a tad jack nicholson and a bit of cesar romero, but with that darkness that the "nolan" batman films all have. and i think that is what makes them more believable, yet still comic book in their own way.

it's such a shame that heath died, as he could really have gone far, not only with this character, but in films in general. he certainly left on a high!

i do like fox too. played by the super cool morgan freeman. he was a new character for me and may have appeared in the comics, but i don't know. either way, i think that he was a good addition to the films and in this one he came in to it a bit more. his characters presence seemed to answer some of the questions about the gadgets in use, done in a "q" from 'james bond' kind of way. it's bits like this that improve a film. i hate it when the hero can just knock up a quick weapon all of a sudden, but fox's resources and skills add to the films and the gadgets credibility.

the replacement of katie holmes with maggie gyllenhall was a good choice too, as they are so similar i barely noticed. they also didn't get too hung up on the romance and make things unnecessarily soppy. knowing that he has something to fight for is enough.

i also like the fact that they addressed the mobility issues with the suit, again it added to the credibility. it's like they listened to the fans and critics and adjusted, to fix what might have been wrong before, although he still seemed to struggle to speak when wearing the head piece.

there are only a couple of elements that didn't work for me. at the end of the party for instance, it was left a bit open as to what happened, which was untidy. there was another bit too, but i've forgotten it, which means that it can't have been that important and i'm just nit picking.

this series as a whole was made to be so much darker and scarier, which i believe was the right choice. it's actually really tense too and had me rapt with attention. the only thing that i would criticise properly is that this one was a bit long, but i'm really not sure where it could have been cut?

it's such a clever story, but maybe there were a few too many good ideas and some could have been saved for another film, although they're all delivered well and appropriately to the story and again i wouldn't know which one to cut out, because they did all work so well.

it's just that a lot of things happen in just one film. if i'd watched it at the cinema, i might have missed the end, because i wouldn't have been able to sit for that long without a wee.

a lot of people would favour this one over "begins", but although the joker is iconic here and brilliantly mad, i think the origin story of batman himself just wins as the best of this trilogy. this one is not far behind and still scores highly though.

900.55/1000.

many hold this in regard as the best superhero-movie of all time, and has given other movies in this genre the biggest shoes ever to fill. i myself believe that to be kind of unfair, since this is not what i would immediately classify as a superhero-movie, simply because it has batman in it. because nolan is such a master at mixing intelligent themes and high-quality entertainment together, he took one of the most iconic superheroes in history and made him a human being in a realistic world, where nothing really is to over the top: no doomsday-devices or superpowers, just a masked vigilante who needs to combat organized crime and the anarchy within the very people he fights for to protect them. he and david s goyer wrote a complex and layered script with deep characters, and made one of the darkest and well-made crime-noir movies i have ever seen(and i don't even like that genre)

acting:

christian bale continues to prove that he is a fantastic actor, with a subtle and laid-back performance as bruce wayne and a harsh and brutal portrayal of a struggling caped crusader. this is not his best role, not by a long shot, but i can imagine that ben affleck was pretty nervous to replace this man.

heath ledger, what more can we say about his real that hasn't already been said? in his final role, he delivered one of the most impressive method-acting roles you will ever encounter, with all odd mannerisms, a creepy voice and laugh, and an enigmatic character that steals every scene. oscar was well deserved.

aaron eckhart was the absolute surprise of this movie. given how few good movies the guy has actually been in, it is a relief and a shame at the same time that he will only be remembered for this role. he gives a down-to-earth, sassy and yet intense performance as a white knight who falls into the abyss of insanity. i believed bruce wayne when he said that with a man like aaron's character, his batman would no longer be needed.

gary oldman's role as jim gordon gets expanded in this sequel, showing a grim and hard-working commissioner who suffers just as much from the consequenses of underestimating the joker as the other protagonists. the man gives a great performance.

maggie gyllenhaal as rachel is a slight improvement over katie holmes, who wasn't very interesting in batman begins, but still her character feels like little more than the damsel in distress, and the few words of wisdom and advice that she gives are not nearly enough to compensate for her lack of likability.

veteran actors like morgan freeman and michael caine play their part, and they do it well. i can't help but miss the emotional core that was much more present in batman begins with these two characters. the sound of their soothing deep voices is enough though to appreciate every scene that they are in.

direction: christopher nolan always has a very clear vision and approach to his movies, and this firm grip is visible throughout the entire movie. the tension and weight is felt in every scene, and even the more lighthearted moments are handled very well.

cinematography: wally pfister, who has worked with nolan on multiple occasions, has switched drastically in style when compared to batman begins. the muddy, brown aesthetic of gotham in that movie has been replaced with a moody grey, while still maintaining the dark shadowy feel that is associated with batman. the dialogue scenes in particular are shot very well on steady-cam, and draw your attention immediately. overall, this is great work.

music: hans zimmer and james newton howard collaborate for a second time for a batman movie, and hans brought a harsher and more electronical element into the score. the old themes from batman begins are still there, but more expanded, and with a harrowing theme for the joker that sets you on edge the more you hear it pop up. as a score to listen to without the movie, it isn't that solid, but it is essential to the atmosphere of this picture and zimmer and howard should receive high praise for this.

plot: david s goyer and nolan wrote a complex and dark movie that can become confusing if not careful. that being said, the execution is brilliantly done, with many twists and turns, and surprisingly relevant questions are brought to light.

editing: this ties directly into the plot, and is the main reason why this movie succeeds so well in its execution: because of the complex structure, good editing is necessary, and lee smith absolutely delivered in that department. particulary the scene transitions after powerful emotional moments are exceptionally well done.

sound: the old sounds from batman begins are back, including batmobile and gadgets, and now also including the high-speed humm of the batpod and the unique-sounding explosions that you don't really come across in other movies. it is not outstanding, but very pleasant for your ears.

production design: even though the setting of this movie appears quite normal, nathan crowley spend an extraordinary amount of detail on the sets and props, making them all feel realistic and gotham like a real city.

costumes&make-up: batman's dark suit is the best version yet, picturing batman as a frightening and looming presence without the need to move a muscle. the joker is exactly what you'd imagine he would look like. so, perfect.

vfx: nolan uses cgi as little as possible, which is a rarity nowadays, and the major exception is two-face. like inception, nolan aims for the perfect blend of digital and the real thing, and when you look at the horrifying imagery, it is really hard to believe that it is not real. chapeau!

tone: the darkest batman movie thus far, largely in thanks to the joker and his schemes, which have such gruesome consequences that the desperation and fear easily carries over from the screen to the audience. the tension is masterfully handled throughout scenes, and a scene in an interrogation room particulary transcends it to a whole new level.

overall concensus:

while not all characters and actors are as charismatic as they should be, heath ledger and the complex script, together with masterful editing and direction, elevate nolan as one of the best filmmakers working today.

the dark knight is a 2008 superhero film directed by christopher nolan from a screenplay he co-wrote with his brother jonathan. the film is based on the dc comics superhero batman, is the sequel to batman begins (2005) and the second installment in the dark knight trilogy. the plot follows vigilante batman, police lieutenant james gordon, and district attorney harvey dent who form an alliance to dismantle organized crime in gotham city. their efforts are derailed by joker, an anarchistic mastermind who seeks to test how far batman will go to save the city from complete chaos. the ensemble cast includes christian bale, michael caine, heath ledger, gary oldman, aaron eckhart, maggie gyllenhaal, and morgan freeman.

warner bros. pictures prioritized a sequel following the successful reinvention of the batman film series with batman begins. nolan and batman begins co-writer david s. goyer developed the story elements, making dent the central protagonist and tragic hero who is caught up in the battle between batman and joker. in writing the screenplay, the nolans were influenced by 1980s batman comics and crime-drama films, and sought to continue batman begins' heightened reality tone. from april to november 2007, filming took place with a $185 million budget in chicago and hong kong, and on sets in england. the dark knight was the first major motion picture to be filmed with high-resolution imax cameras. nolan avoided using computer-generated imagery unless necessary, insisting on practical stunts including the flipping of an 18-wheel truck and the blowing-up of a factory.

an all star cast including christian bale, gary oldman, morgan freeman, michael caine & the late, great heath ledger amongst others!

batman faces off against the joker & gothams underworld as chaos ensues as the joker makes several attempts to destabilise gotham by doing things such as murder, armed robbery & kidnap etc.

things take an even more troublesome turn when district attorney & bruce wayne's friend harvey dent & his wife rachel are both kidnapped & strapped to timed explosives in separate locations across gotham leaving batman to choose which one of them to save!

batman chooses harvey who's face becomes badly disfigured in the explosion that occurs as he escapes with batman's help. when harvey wakes up in hospital & discovers his wife is dead then he embarks on a mission to make all those he holds responsible for rachel's death pay for their part in the crimes leading up to it!

an awesome film & by far my favourite batman film, i highly recommend watching this if you haven't already!

the greatest crime movie ever created is the dark knight! the ensemble is excellent; michael caine, christian bale, heath ledger, gary oldman, morgan freeman, and aaron eckhart all gave outstanding performances. heath's acting and facial gestures are amazing! this is an iconic movie with an imaginative narrative! the sole nolan movie with a straight plot is this one.

there are a ton of surprises in this movie, so you never know what will happen next. the best side characters, villains, and heroes. each has a compelling character arc. the joker and batman costumes are beautifully designed. two-face and joker have incredible makeup as well. the movie's message is masterfully written.

the dialogue is excellent. some quotes will always stick with me. there are a few funny moments but no laughs because the movie is quite serious, which i found to be enjoyable. the hindi dubbing is excellent. hans zimmer created incredible music that perfectly captures the mood and feel of the movie. choosing to give batman and the joker separate soundtracks is a wise choice. through the credible gotham city, the movie realistically depicts the sinister world of crime. this film is renowned in every scene and is not to be missed. one of the most exquisite conclusions to a live-action movie is this one. this is the most flawless movie i have ever seen, with the greatest beginning and conclusion.

the dark knight was an amazing movie of my generation to see. i enjoyed watching this film with family and friends. the joker played an excellent role. i'll more than likely promote this film to others. i remember the scene where batman made a surprise to a few of the joker crooks and shown them why they shouldn't mess with batman. christian bale gave a awesome performance for the project. the layout of this film was been great with good follow ups. it definitely brings everyone back to the childhood days of the original batman series. christian bale and morgan freeman create a awesome team to work with together to get rid of the troubles of gotham city. this film is a film i'll recommend to family and friends.

this is the second film of the christopher nolan's trilogy, and here batman will face one of his most famous villains: joker. the film has screenplay by christopher nolan (who also ensures the direction) and jonathan nolan. it has the participation of christian bale, michael caine, aaron eckhart, morgan freeman, maggie gyllenhaal, gary oldman and heath ledger.

this film follows on from "batman begins", keeping more or less the same team and achieving a good unit with the previous film, which prevented the great continuity failures that infest sequels and sequential films. this is an psychological action movie with great scenes, dramatic moments and a good dose of special visual and sound effects that help to intensify the events but manage to avoid having too much prominence. the actors were up to the challenge and toasted the audience with flawless performances, although there aren't able to surprise as much as the first film. aaron eckhart deserves congratulations by giving his character a very particular and intense psychological wealth and bale, one of the actors that stands out naturally by having the leading role, makes a very complete performance, worthy of an actor who has reached maturity and eagerly want to fight for stardom and the massive recognition. congratulations. but this cast was almost overshadowed by a thunderous heath ledger. this actor wore the coat of joker perfectly, embodying a character who has undergone a great reevaluation in this film, and that ledger, with this sublime performance, will probably mark for decades. it was the best farewell to this actor, a promise of hollywood that we never get to see develop due to his sudden death.

few films have achieved the same level of critical acclaim and enduring popularity as the dark knight. released in 2008, christopher nolan's sequel to batman begins stands as a testament to the power of storytelling, performance, and technical mastery. with its complex characters, thought-provoking themes, and visually stunning action sequences, the dark knight has captivated audiences worldwide and cemented its place as one of the greatest superhero films of all time.

the film follows the caped crusader's relentless pursuit of the enigmatic criminal mastermind known as the joker, a role that heath ledger delivers with chilling intensity. ledger's portrayal of the joker is a masterclass in acting, capturing the character's chaotic energy, unpredictable nature, and profound nihilism. the joker's presence serves as a stark counterpoint to batman's unwavering commitment to justice, creating a dynamic that is as thrilling as it is thought-provoking.

nolan's direction is impeccable, weaving together a complex narrative that explores the darker side of human nature, the blurred lines between hero and villain, and the very nature of the batman mythos. the film is visually stunning, with cinematographer wally pfister capturing gotham city in all its gritty realism and grandeur. the action sequences are expertly choreographed and executed, delivering a visceral thrill that is both exhilarating and grounded in reality.

the performances across the board are exceptional, with christian bale delivering a subtly nuanced performance as batman, conveying the character's inner turmoil and unwavering determination. michael caine is equally captivating as alfred pennyworth, batman's loyal butler and confidant. morgan freeman shines as lucius fox, the resourceful and brilliant technological genius who provides batman with the tools he needs to fight crime.

the dark knight is not just a superhero film; it is a cinematic masterpiece that explores profound themes of morality, justice, and the nature of evil. it is a film that will stay with you long after the credits roll, challenging your perceptions and leaving you questioning the line between good and evil. with its complex characters, thought-provoking themes, and visually stunning action sequences, the dark knight is a must-see for any fan of cinema.

in the world of comic books, there is a superhero sequel that stands out from the rest. batman is facing a dangerous enemy who is causing destruction throughout gotham city. the villain's performance is captivating and is considered one of the greatest in cinematic history. there are many memorable moments in the movie, such as batman's use of unconventional weapons and his encounter with a school bus. the presence of bat groupies and gordon's exceptional portrayal also add to the intrigue.

batman's acting style is urgent and is complemented by the legendary sir michael caine. the absence of katie holmes is notable, and harvey dent's distinctive hair and courtroom drama are memorable. there is a choice between maggie and katie, and the presence of red redding, julia roberts's older brother, adds a unique element. the joker's unsettling nature and the iconic question "why so serious?" repeated thrice emphasize his menacing persona.

batman has a bat cellphone, and there is a revelation that bats can fly. there is also a bat airplane jet, and bruce wayne is skilled at riding a motorcycle. the joker has a distinctive calling card, and there are no joke home videos. batman participates in a bat fundraiser, and the concept of dna hijacking is introduced. there is a hypothetical battle between christian bale, adam west, and lego batman, and the film features bat extortion and a breakfast club geek.

the joker's explosive finger guns and use of a shotgun are memorable. there is a pivotal vote, and the battle of the boats, and morgan freeman provides wisdom in the movie. the importance of an ace is stressed, and there is a symbolic joker fly. christian bale's portrayal is commendable, and christopher nolan's direction is masterful. the film is forever linked to heath ledger, who gave an unforgettable performance as the joker.

the 2nd installment in nolan's dark knight trilogy. what makes this movie great is despite being a cat and mouse chase like a typical crime thriller is that it's between batman and joker. this two are one of the most popular and best written fictional characters not only in comicbook but overall in fiction.

the side characters also gave great performance especially gar oldman as commissioner gordon and morgan freeman as fox.

overall this movie is a flawless masterpiece and will always be remembered as the 'greatest superhero movie of all time'

there is nothing comic book about the masterful the dark knight. this is a serious film grounded mostly in a real world setting. but at the same time - it never deviates from the original concept of good v bad. what it does is layer this with philosophical questions throughout. the blurred line between villain and hero has never been explored better than here. the acting is first class especially ledger as the joker and eckhart as harvey dent. caine and freeman deliver as usual. the zimmer score is brilliant as are many action set pieces. the balance between deep layers of story and entertainment is achieved. the unforgettable performance by ledger as the villain is the perfect vehicle for the film to explore the very nature of the different ways evil can look like and perhaps a parallel can be drawn with the hero batman. one of the best movies of the 2000s.

at the heart of "the dark knight" is the mesmerizing performance of heath ledger as the joker. ledger's portrayal of the iconic villain is nothing short of legendary, as he immerses himself completely into the role, delivering a chilling and unforgettable performance that earned him a posthumous academy award for best supporting actor. the joker's chaotic presence serves as a perfect foil to christian bale's brooding batman, creating a dynamic and compelling conflict that drives the narrative forward.

but "the dark knight" isn't just about its iconic villains; it's also a testament to the power of heroism in the face of darkness. bale's portrayal of bruce wayne/batman is at once vulnerable and commanding, as he grapples with his own inner demons while striving to protect gotham city from the joker's reign of terror. supported by an exceptional cast, including michael caine, gary oldman, and morgan freeman, bale's performance anchors the film with emotional depth and gravitas.

nolan's direction is nothing short of masterful, as he crafts a gritty and atmospheric world that feels both grounded and larger-than-life. the film's stunning visuals, pulse-pounding action sequences, and haunting score by hans zimmer combine to create an immersive cinematic experience that leaves a lasting impression.

at its core, "the dark knight" is a thought-provoking exploration of morality, justice, and the nature of heroism. through its complex characters and morally ambiguous dilemmas, the film challenges audiences to confront the darkness within themselves and consider what it truly means to be a hero.

in conclusion, "the dark knight" is more than just a superhero film; it's a cinematic masterpiece that continues to captivate audiences with its timeless themes, unforgettable performances, and unparalleled storytelling. christopher nolan's vision, coupled with heath ledger's iconic portrayal of the joker, ensures that "the dark knight" will be remembered as a true classic of modern cinema.

in 2005, director christopher nolan gave the ailing batman franchise a successful reboot with the very well made 'batman begins', and of course it was very well received. a sequel was, naturally, always going to be on the cards and it's been delivered in the form of the dark knight; a film that follows on directly from the first film and manages to continue the story in a way that is interesting and at times frightening, and does it better than the first film did. once again we focus on gotham city. things have started to change for the better as more and more criminals are being taken off the street. this is thanks in part to the mysterious masked marauder known as batman; but police officer jim gordon and district attorney harvey dent are also partly to thank. however, things are plunged into chaos when the joker enters the fray and begins to shake things up; specifically going after batman. batman soon realises he must stop the joker and his wave of terror at all costs; but the battle may push him to his very limits.

batman begins was all about showing the creation of bruce wayne and batman and my biggest problem with it was that the film really lacked a definite villain. having got the character creation out of way, this leaves director christopher nolan free to explore other characters and areas of the plot, and it pays off very well indeed. there are a lot of different characters and elements to the story and things move very quickly; but the skillful way that the film is presented ensures that the important elements are focused on enough. the success of the film is thanks mostly to the fantastic joker character and the director's willingness to take the film further than you would expect a comic book movie to go. the joker is a thoroughly dark villain; a maniacal anarchistic psychopath who goes round forcing blades into people's mouths and blowing things up, and this gives the film a very dark edge. the tone of the movie is also very skilfully handled; nolan portrays the efforts of the crime fighters in making the city a better place to live, so when things are actually plunged into chaos - we feel bad for the people living in the city - which is pretty impressive when you consider that gotham city is a fictional place.

a lot of the hype surrounding this movie was due to the unfortunate premature death of heath ledger. i have to admit that i've not seen a great deal of his earlier performances but this last performance really highlights what a great loss his death was for cinema. heath ledger creates a villain that, while distinctively comic book; is also very real and frightening for that reason. he completely owns every scene he's in and this is a performance that will go down in history as one of the greatest antagonists on film. the rest of the cast is very good too. gary oldman, michael caine and morgan freeman all step into their roles from the first film effectively and provide good performances, while christian bale continues to provide the 'perfect; batman; although for me he's even better simply as bruce wayne. maggie gyllenhaal replaces katie holmes as the love interest is even better in the role. she's not a natural beauty, but she was easy enough on my eyes and always convinces as a female lawyer. aaron eckhart is the biggest standout outside of ledgar, however, with his turn as harvey dent. i wasn't impressed with him (or anything else) in the black dahlia; but here he hits the upstanding politician nail directly on the head and manages to make us care about his character.

despite being based on a comic book, everything in the film is taken very seriously and the characters are one of the most important things about it. as you would expect, there's plenty of action and fighting too; and the two come into balance very well to ensure that the dark knight works as a complete whole. naturally, all the hype surrounding the film does go just a little too far - but there's no denying that this is a definite triumph on the whole and deserves its place as one of the best comic book films ever made.

before we begin, i'd like to reveal something about myself. i am not a fan of batman. that is not to say i dislike batman, but i have never been especially driven to seek out adventures and merchandise pertaining to gotham's favourite costumed watchdog. prior to seeing knight, the only two batman movies i have seen in full are batman and robin and batman begins. i'm not about to pass harsh judgment on either - i admit b&r was quite amusing in a rather unintentional way and that batman begins was a well-crafted film (but i do not consider it to be a masterpiece in any way). at the very least, it set the bar high for its successor, and rather high up at that.

i know there's a thread floating around here with the first five minutes of knight in it. i never looked at it here, seeing it for the first time on an imax screen. this opening scene alone - which follows a bank robbery, and that is all i shall say about it - gives a very good indication of just how highly knight sets its own bar. it burns its way into your head and lets you know that the next two-and-a-half hours are going to be quite a step up from what you were probably expecting.

plot-wise, you should have a fairly good idea what's going on. there's batman and there's the joker and there's the usual kind of plot complications that dog the "superhero sequel", namely the whole act of strongly humanising the hero (just like all the other "2" movies). i'm not about to deride knight for its few clichéd plot devices - show me a blockbuster sequel without them. it's what the plot gets surrounded with that will truly impress you.

first off, the acting. a serious sequel demands very strong character development. seeing as a lot of you are hardened moviegoers, you no doubt already know that. of course, knight sticks to this "rule". but how it does is impressive. the cast is impressive. aside from strong returns from caine, oldman and freeman, you have the introduction of a handful of new characters that will stick around in viewers' memories longer than, say, the scarecrow.

obviously, the first thing to come to mind is the joker. naturally i was wary of all the hype surrounding heath ledger's oh-so-epic final role. could it really be as good as everybody was saying? the answer is a loud and hearty yes. ledger is quite simply a showstopper. he steals more scenes than the joker steals loot. his presence is simply commanding. right from one of the earliest scenes (which i won't spoil with anything other than the phrase "magic trick") he takes hold and doesn't let go. whether this talk of an oscar is far-fetched or not, i can honestly see a nomination happening. i kept thinking to myself, "this is ledger?" and when an actor is capable of doing that, well that is a good actor indeed. now i can see how much of a tragedy his death truly is.

the other character of note is aaron eckhart as harvey dent (best known to fans for becoming two-face). granted, eckhart does not do as much show-stealing as ledger, but his performance is carefully played and very convincing as he goes through a number of stages, from smooth and trusty to thinly veiled psychopathy. when his transformation into two-face is revealed, it is one hell of a shock (and a damned good effects job).

ironically, for a movie titled the dark knight, it seems like christian bale as the eponymous character is overshadowed by the aforementioned examples. granted, this is because bale is quite simply not a showboating kind of actor (at least in my experience), and that makes a fine contrast to the joker's wild streak. also, maggie gyllenhaal doesn't really make that much of a better rachel than katie holmes did, but it's a forgivable flaw in an otherwise brilliant spot of casting.

of course, being a summer blockbuster (or winter, as the case may be), it just wouldn't be a superhero movie without a hefty helping of action sequences. the action is par for the course - there's chases, fights, even a couple of handfuls of suspenseful "beat-the-clock" moments. there are a handful of moments which induce laughs or a collective "whoa" from the audience (namely, the batpod). the inclusion of the joker and his penchant for playing tricks make for some truly interesting setpieces, especially the "social experiment" he pulls near the climax.

then we get to the ending. while it's not a cliffhanger, it really does end on a rather ambiguous note (kind of like the road warrior did) which sort of leaves it open for a third film, but at the same time doesn't, if that makes any sense. it could've been handled better, i suppose, but it's all about leaving them wanting more and the ending - which shows that things are only going to get much worse for batman - certainly illustrates that.

the dark knight really did manage to pull off a miracle. it lived up to all of its hype (both pre- and post-ledger's demise) and it indicates that not all blockbusters are going to pot. the only problem i can see this creating is that if there is a third instalment in this new trilogy (which, in all probability, there will be) it probably will not manage to top this one. this will be a one-of-a-kind, and who knows, maybe in 30 years' time when people are talking about which sequels were better than the original, the first movie to pop up will be the dark knight.

when christopher nolan directed his first film, doodlebug, in 1997, i'm sure he had no idea that a decade later he would be directing the box-office blowout, the dark knight. the film beat out spider-man 3 for the biggest weekend opener in the box office, and also surpassed box office records set by movies such as¬¬¬¬¬¬¬ ¬¬¬¬star wars, and e.t. the extra terrestrial. the dark knight is currently trailing titanic for the total box office record by a mere $80 million. eighty million sure sounds like a lot, but keep in mind: the dark knight has only been in theaters since mid-july, whereas titanic sailed in the box office for nine months.

the film's great success can be mostly attributed to the acting style of the late heath ledger. ledger, who took on the role of the joker in the summer smash, spent very much time studying the 1928 silent film, the man who laughs. it is also rumored that in order to prepare to take on the role, ledger spent much time in front of the bathroom mirror practicing his smile and laugh.

while most may argue that ledger is the main feature of the film, viewers must not forget about the other talent found in the movie. the new chapter of the caped crusader also contains other notable actors such as lead christian bale as bruce wayne and alter-ego batman, morgan freeman as lucius fox, the batman equivalent of james bond's 'q', aaron eckhart as colleague harvey dent, and cillian murphy, who appears briefly as scarecrow.

containing cutting-edge special effects, the film is full of explosions, catastrophes, and a couple of intricate chase scenes. though the film was shot in the famous chi-town, director nolan was seemingly careful not to include any big chicago landmarks such as navy pier, millennium park, or the skyline, giving the film a more not-of-this-world appearance.

batman is viewed by gotham city as a masked vigilante whose help only appears to result in the deaths of policemen and other prominent figures. entering the scene, the joker does nothing to help this perceived image, as he frustrates both bruce wayne and the audience with his clever attacks on both society and the dark knight's social status.

the story goes beyond your classic, 'good-guy, bad-guy' ideals and replaces these with things that you wouldn't expect such as the importance of love over friendship, and the concept of revenge. batman is torn between business acquaintance harvey dent and one-time lover rachel dawes, notably played by maggie gyllenhal, who took the role in the stead of katie holmes.

the dark knight is a classic example of the shift in audience interest from bright and cheery movies to more dark and dreary films. somewhere between the joker's devious plots and society's misunderstandings about the caped crusader's intentions, the dark knight will leave you gaping, wondering where the last two hours of your life disappeared to.

"i think audiences get too comfortable and familiar in today's movies. they believe everything they're hearing and seeing. i like to shake that up." -christopher nolan

leading up to seeing this movie, i had read dozens of reviews, mostly of praise for "the dark knight". but amongst the praise was critiques, and there were many reviews with the same critiques, making me worried this movie would only be good because of it's flaws. one of the mentioned flaws was that this film was very slow paced. i don't know what movies some reviewers saw, but though this is long, it is not slow paced, in fact, you could say it's the exact opposite. especially towards the beginning, this is a fast paced movie, with lots of action. along with that, it's one of the best movies of the year, and though it may sound clichéd to say this in a dark knight review, heath ledger will be remembered for this role, if any, as his finest moment(s) on the silver screen.

gotham city is in peril, and the only person who can save it is...harvey dent. new district attorney harvey dent is bringing men to justice and throwing them in the clink, sometimes by the hundreds. harvey's got a great girl, bruce wayne's (christian bale) old flame, rachel dawes (now played by maggie gyllenhall). the joker (heath ledger) is the new psycopath in town, and batman, or harvey dent must stop him.

what makes the dark knight so great is how well it works as both a superhero movie, and an action drama. if this wasn't a batman movie, it would still be a fantastic action flick, not to say batman is a throw away character, because he certainly isn't. the direction is very good, though there are a few action scenes that could have been filmed better.

heath ledger is the performance that makes the movie, not because this was the movie that led to his unfortunate demise, but because he was amazing and captivating. whether or not he will win best supporting actor, he still has gotten critical acclaim for his portrayal of the psychopath. his performance is not a let down, he is just great. the other actors all do well too. normally i think of aaron eckhart as being a b-movie actor, but here he shows what makes him a star. christian bale is good as bruce wayne, and okay as batman. that annoying scratchy voice is, well, annoying. it's overused. batman even uses it to talk to people that know he is bruce wayne. maybe the suit cuts off his lungs or something. maggie gyllenhall is a fine actress in the role, though for varying reasons it felt a bit off having her playing rachel. michael caine and morgan freeman added a lot in supporting roles, and gary oldman plays a heck of a officer/commissioner gordon.

now onto the negatives. the beginning of the movie had way too many short scenes of random characters that it felt like an anthology, and it didn't explain itself well enough until later. when the scenes began to be longer and stopped jumping from character to character, the movie got much better. one element missing from the film is drama that connects with the audience. drama was plentiful, but i never felt connected with the characters enough to care what happens, probably because of the fast cut opening that helped to underdevelop the characters until later in the film.

i miss danny elfman. his musical score brought life to the first two batman films, and the musical score here is just loud and annoying and adds nothing. hans zimmer and james newton howard are talented, so what were they doing here? overall, this was one of the better batman movies, and is also one of the best movies of the year. it's not perfect, but perfection is hard to find, and even in it's imperfection, it outshines most movies this year.

my rating: *** 1/2 out of ****. 145 mins. pg-13 for violence.

i just got back from seeing this movie, and in a word: marvelous. heath ledger was even better than the hype. i found myself anxiously awaiting his next screen appearance. morgan freeman, gary oldman, and michael caine were all stellar in their respective roles, but i was pleasantly surprised by aaron eckhart's harvey "two-face" dent. overall, he was very convincing and held his ground in a movie full of excellent performances.

the action and fight sequences were all very well done, and i disagree with some of the statements that this didn't have enough of batman kicking butt, because it certainly had plenty. it also had one of the coolest opening scenes in recent history, in my opinion. there were some new bat-gadgets thrown in as well, which was good to see. the cinematography was absolutely spectacular. some of the overhead and tracking shots were simply outstanding and helped to give the movie its grand scale.

as for the downfalls, the movie is a tad long. while it never drags, i think they could have trimmed the fat. (excluding any joker scenes, of course.) christian bale's batman voice got annoying a couple of times, but it doesn't really detract from the movie and he's so great besides that so i won't hold it against him. maggie gyllenhaal, while not as terrible as everyone said she was, definitely could have been better. my last complaint is that the ending, while great, didn't leave as much anticipation for the next movie (assuming there is one) as batman begins did. overall...

rating: 9/10 - certainly a must-see for any fan of batman, and fans of movies for that matter.
